meta.blurb: Caesar builds a wall around a city, then a second wall facing outward, because a huge army of Gauls is coming to rescue it. Before Alesia come a bridge over the Rhine and two landings in Britain, all told by Caesar himself.
meta.bible:
Julius Caesar: the Roman governor and general who wrote the book; he writes about himself in the third person, calm and clear, and he always makes his own choices sound wise. Gaul: the land that is now mostly France and Belgium, split into three parts. Gauls: the Celtic peoples of Gaul. Belgae: the northern Gauls, whom Caesar calls the bravest. Helvetii: a people of what is now Switzerland who tried to move west in 58 BC. Orgetorix: the Helvetian noble who began the plan. Divico: an old Helvetian leader. Ariovistus: the German king in Gaul. Aedui: Gauls who were allies of Rome. Remi: Belgic allies of Rome. Nervii: the fiercest Belgic people. Atuatuci: a Belgic people. Veneti: a seafaring people of Brittany. Usipetes and Tencteri: German tribes who crossed the Rhine. Germans: the peoples east of the Rhine. Britons: the people of Britain. Cassivellaunus: the British leader north of the Thames. Ambiorix: the chief of the Eburones who destroyed a Roman force in winter. Eburones: his people. Sabinus and Cotta: the Roman commanders killed by Ambiorix. Quintus Cicero: a Roman commander whose camp was besieged. Labienus: Caesar's best officer. Vercingetorix: the young Arvernian who unites the Gauls in 52 BC. Arverni: his people. Dumnorix: an Aeduan noble who plots against Caesar. Mandubii: the people of Alesia. Druids: the priests and teachers of the Gauls. Hirtius: the officer who wrote the eighth book after Caesar. Legion: a Roman army unit of about five thousand men. Cohort: a tenth of a legion. Centurion: an officer of a hundred men. Standard-bearer: the soldier who carries the legion's eagle. Province: a land ruled by Rome. Cavalry: soldiers on horses. Rampart: a wall of earth. Siege: surrounding a town to take it. Tribute: money paid to a stronger people. Rome, Italy, Geneva, the Rhône, the Saône, Bibracte, the Aisne, the Sabis, Britain, the Thames, the Rhine, Cenabum, Avaricum, Gergovia, Lutetia, Alesia, Uxellodunum, Brittany, the Cévennes, the Hercynian Forest: the places. Dates are BC: the war runs from 58 to 51; the first crossing to Britain is 55; the second is 54; Alesia is 52. Numbers are Caesar's own and are often too big, and the text says so. Voice and tone: brisk, clear and confident, like a good report from the field; wars are told without gore. Added names: Aquitani: the people of the south-west of Gaul. Celts: the people of the middle of Gaul. Garonne, Marne, Seine, Loire, Meuse, Doubs, Aisne, Jura, Alps, Vesontio, Noviodunum, Bibrax, Octodurus, Atuatuca, Sabis, Cevennes, Elaver, Allier, Cenabum, Avaricum, Gergovia, Lutetia, Agedincum, Metiosedum, Melodunum, Alesia, Uxellodunum, Lugdunum, Portus Itius, Kent, Aquitania: the places. Casticus: the Sequanian noble in Orgetorix's plot. Rauraci, Tulingi, Latobrigi, Boii, Santones, Tigurini, Lingones, Verbigeni, Suessiones, Bellovaci, Ambiani, Atrebates, Viromandui, Harudes, Suebi, Ubii, Sugambri, Cimbri, Teutones, Unelli, Treveri, Carnutes, Senones, Parisii, Aulerci, Bituriges, Trinovantes: peoples. Liscus: the chief magistrate of the Aedui. Diviciacus: Dumnorix's brother, a loyal friend of Rome. Considius: the scout who wrongly said the hill was held by Gauls. Procillus and Mettius: Caesar's envoys, chained by Ariovistus. Marius: the Roman general who beat the Cimbri and Teutones. Publius Crassus: the young cavalry commander. Servius Galba, Decimus Brutus, Gaius Volusenus, Cato, Cicero, Mark Antony, Trebonius, Fabius, Baculus, Petronius, Petrosidius, Pullo, Vorenus, Piso, Cassius: Romans. Iccius: a leader of the Remi. Commius: an Atrebatian chief, Caesar's friend. Cassivellaunus, Mandubracius, Cingetorix, Carvilius, Taximagulus, Segovax: Britons. Catuvolcus: the other chief of the Eburones. Indutiomarus: the Treveran chief. Acco: a Gaulish chief put to death. Celtillus: Vercingetorix's father. Lucterius, Litaviccus, Convictolitavis, Eporedorix, Viridomarus, Vercassivellaunus, Critognatus, Camulogenus, Drappes, Correus: Gaulish leaders. Mercury, Apollo, Mars, Jupiter, Minerva: gods. Claudius: the Roman emperor born in Lugdunum.
Pompey: the Roman general and politician who lent Caesar a legion. Cherusci: a German people. Bacenis: a forest. Ardennes: a forest in the north of Gaul.
Pictones, Cadurci, Turoni, Lemovices, Andes, Helvii, Gabali: peoples of Gaul. Clodius: a Roman politician murdered in 52 BC. Narbo: a city of the Roman Province. Vellaunodunum: a town. Gaius Fufius Cita: the Roman officer killed at Cenabum.
Teutomatus: king of the Nitiobriges. Nitiobriges: a people of Gaul.
Sedulius: a leader of the Lemovices.
chapters: The Day Caesar Took a Shield

beats.scene: A Roman general studies a map of Gaul divided into three parts
beats.summary: Caesar opens by saying that Gaul is divided into three parts, each with its own people.

beats.scene: Warriors of the Belgae stand on a northern shore far from Roman traders
beats.summary: Caesar says the Belgae are the bravest because they live farthest from Roman trade and comfort.

beats.scene: A rich noble in a fur cloak speaks to a mountain crowd
beats.summary: Orgetorix, the richest Helvetian, persuades his people to leave their narrow homeland.

beats.scene: Helvetian men build wagons and stack sacks of grain in a valley
beats.summary: The Helvetii spend two years preparing, and Orgetorix makes secret pacts with Casticus and Dumnorix.

beats.scene: Helvetian nobles call a prisoner before a crowd for trial
beats.summary: The plot is betrayed, Orgetorix is put on trial, and he dies before the verdict.

beats.scene: Whole families watch their village burn as loaded wagons roll away
beats.summary: The Helvetii burn their towns and villages and set out regardless.

beats.scene: A Roman officer counts clay tablets covered in Greek letters
beats.summary: In the Helvetian camp the Romans find a list that counts 368,000 people.

beats.scene: A long line of wagons waits beside a lake below snowy mountains
beats.summary: The Helvetii choose the shorter road through the Roman Province, beside the Rhône.

beats.scene: A messenger hands Caesar a letter in a busy Roman street
beats.summary: News of the march reaches Caesar in Rome, and he sees the danger to the Province.

beats.scene: Caesar rides hard along a dusty road toward the Rhône
beats.summary: Caesar leaves Rome and hurries to Further Gaul, where he has only one legion.

beats.scene: Roman soldiers chop down a wooden bridge over a fast river at Geneva
beats.summary: Caesar cuts the bridge at Geneva and tells the Helvetian envoys to come back in two weeks.

beats.scene: A long earth wall with forts and a ditch runs beside a wide river
beats.summary: Caesar's soldiers build a wall sixteen feet high and nearly nineteen miles long along the Rhône.

beats.scene: Helvetian men push rafts into a river as Roman soldiers throw javelins
beats.summary: Refused permission, the Helvetii try to cross by force, and the wall beats them.

beats.scene: Dumnorix shakes hands with Sequani leaders while wagons wait in a pass
beats.summary: Dumnorix wins the Sequani's agreement to let the Helvetii cross the narrow pass of the Jura.

beats.scene: Caesar crosses snowy Alpine hills at the head of five legions
beats.summary: Caesar leaves Labienus at the wall, raises more legions in Italy and returns over the Alps.

beats.scene: A burning farm stands in a field while Aeduan farmers run for safety
beats.summary: The Helvetii ruin the fields of the Aedui, and the Aedui beg Caesar for help.

beats.scene: Roman soldiers attack a crowd on a river bank at night
beats.summary: Caesar surprises the Tigurini, who are still waiting to cross the Saône, and cuts them down.

beats.scene: Roman engineers hammer a wooden bridge across a slow river in one day
beats.summary: Caesar bridges the Saône in a day, a job that took the Helvetii twenty.

beats.scene: An old Helvetian chief speaks proudly to Caesar on a grassy bank
beats.summary: Divico offers peace on Helvetian terms and warns Caesar about the old Roman defeat.

beats.scene: Caesar listens with folded arms as the old chief shakes his head
beats.summary: Caesar demands hostages, and Divico replies that his people take hostages, they do not give them.

beats.scene: Roman and Helvetian horsemen clash on an open plain
beats.summary: Caesar's cavalry is beaten by only five hundred Helvetian riders, and the Helvetii grow bold.

beats.scene: A Roman column marches along a dusty road behind a distant enemy
beats.summary: Caesar follows the Helvetii for fifteen days, but the grain promised by the Aedui does not come.

beats.scene: An Aeduan magistrate whispers a secret to Caesar in a tent
beats.summary: Liscus tells Caesar that Dumnorix is the one blocking the grain.

beats.scene: A weeping Gaul clasps Caesar's hands to plead for his brother
beats.summary: Diviciacus begs for Dumnorix, and Caesar forgives him but sets guards on him.

beats.scene: A scout on a horse points at a hill as soldiers hold back
beats.summary: A scout wrongly reports that Gauls hold a hill that Labienus has really taken, and the chance is lost.

beats.scene: A deserter gallops across a field toward a Gallic camp
beats.summary: Caesar turns toward Bibracte for food, and the Helvetii turn back to attack him.

beats.scene: Caesar sends his horse away as soldiers form lines on a hill
beats.summary: Caesar sends away every horse so that all share the same danger, then draws up his legions.

beats.scene: Javelins fall from a hill onto a wall of locked shields
beats.summary: Roman javelins break the Helvetian shield wall, and the Helvetii fall back to a hill.

beats.scene: Warriors of the Boii strike a Roman line from the side
beats.summary: The Boii and Tulingi attack the Roman flank, and the battle lasts until night.

beats.scene: Women and children throw stones from a circle of wagons at dusk
beats.summary: The Helvetii fight on behind their wagons, and the Romans take the camp late at night.

beats.scene: Starving Helvetian families hand spears and shields to Roman officers
beats.summary: The Helvetii surrender and are sent home to rebuild; only about 110,000 are left.

beats.scene: Gallic chiefs kneel before Caesar in a tent while one weeps
beats.summary: Gallic chiefs congratulate Caesar, then ask for a secret meeting, and Diviciacus speaks for them.

beats.scene: A Gallic noble points across a river at German wagons and warriors
beats.summary: Diviciacus tells how the Germans came, how many there are now, and what Ariovistus has taken.

beats.scene: A group of silent chiefs stare at the ground in front of Caesar
beats.summary: The Sequani stay silent in fear, and Caesar decides to ask Ariovistus for a meeting.

beats.scene: A German king stands beside his tall wagon and refuses to bow
beats.summary: Ariovistus refuses to come, and answers every Roman demand with the right of war.

beats.scene: A hilltop town almost surrounded by a looping river
beats.summary: Caesar marches day and night to seize Vesontio before Ariovistus can.

beats.scene: Roman officers write their wills by lamplight in a gloomy tent
beats.summary: Stories of giant Germans spread terror through the army at Vesontio.

beats.scene: Caesar speaks sternly to centurions standing in rows in the camp
beats.summary: Caesar scolds his officers and says he will march with the tenth legion alone.

beats.scene: Soldiers of the tenth legion cheer as the army marches out
beats.summary: The tenth legion thanks Caesar, the others are ashamed, and the whole army marches for seven days.

beats.scene: A Roman soldier climbs onto a horse while his friends laugh
beats.summary: Ariovistus asks for a meeting, and Caesar puts soldiers of the tenth legion on the Gauls' horses.

beats.scene: Two leaders on horseback meet on a grassy mound between two armies
beats.summary: On a mound between the camps, Caesar and Ariovistus talk, and the meeting ends when German horsemen throw stones.

beats.scene: Two Roman envoys are led away in chains by German guards
beats.summary: Ariovistus asks for a second meeting, and chains the envoys that Caesar sends instead.

beats.scene: German women read the eddies of a river while warriors wait nearby
beats.summary: The German women forbid a battle before the new moon, and Caesar attacks at once.

beats.scene: Roman soldiers leap onto locked German shields and tear them down
beats.summary: The Romans charge too fast for German spears and break the shield wall by hand.

beats.scene: A young cavalry commander sends a line of soldiers to a struggling wing
beats.summary: Young Publius Crassus sends the third line to save the Roman left, and the Germans break.

beats.scene: A German king pushes a small boat into a wide river at dusk
beats.summary: The Germans flee to the Rhine, and Ariovistus escapes in a small boat.

beats.scene: A bound man is dragged along by guards as Roman horsemen gallop up
beats.summary: Caesar finds Procillus alive in chains, and Procillus tells how the lots saved him.

beats.scene: Soldiers settle into winter tents while snow falls on the mountains
beats.summary: The Suebi go home, and Caesar ends the campaign of 58 BC and leaves for northern Italy.

beats.scene: Gallic chiefs swear oaths over a fire at night
beats.summary: Rumours reach Caesar that the Belgae are plotting, so he raises two more legions.

beats.scene: Roman archers shoot from a hill at warriors beneath a town wall
beats.summary: The Remi join Rome, and Caesar relieves their town of Bibrax with archers and slingers.

beats.scene: A Roman camp on a ridge behind a ditch beside a marsh
beats.summary: Caesar camps on the Aisne with a marsh in front, and the Belgae fail to cross.

beats.scene: A disordered army of Gauls leaves camp at night as Roman riders watch
beats.summary: The hungry Belgae go home in disorder, and Caesar's cavalry cut down the rear.

beats.scene: Gauls on a town wall stare at a tall Roman siege tower
beats.summary: Noviodunum surrenders at the sight of the Roman siege works, and other tribes make peace.

beats.scene: A thick hedge of bent and twisted trees blocks a woodland path
beats.summary: The Nervii, who refuse wine and trade, plan an ambush with their neighbours.

beats.scene: Nervian warriors burst from a wood across a river toward a half-built camp
beats.summary: The Nervii attack at the river Sabis while the Romans are still building their camp.

beats.scene: Roman officers shout orders as soldiers run in different directions
beats.summary: Caesar must do everything at once, and the soldiers have no time to arm properly.

beats.scene: Caesar grabs a shield from a soldier and fights in the front rank
beats.summary: Caesar takes a shield, goes to the front and calls the centurions by name.

beats.scene: Roman soldiers push Gallic warriors down a slope into a river
beats.summary: The Roman left and centre win, but the right is open and the Nervii pour through.

beats.scene: Nervian warriors climb over heaps of fallen men as Roman help arrives
beats.summary: Labienus sends the tenth legion back, and the Nervii are cut down.

beats.scene: Old men, women and children come out of a marsh to meet Caesar
beats.summary: The Nervii are almost destroyed, but Caesar spares the survivors.

beats.scene: Gauls on a high town wall laugh at a tall wooden Roman siege tower
beats.summary: The Atuatuci laugh at the Roman siege tower, then ask for peace when it rolls forward.

beats.scene: Warriors hurl weapons from a wall in a night attack on Roman lines
beats.summary: The Atuatuci break their word and attack at night, and Caesar sells the survivors.

beats.scene: Roman senators in white togas announce thanks as crowds fill a street
beats.summary: Rome decrees fifteen days of thanksgiving, and Crassus brings the Atlantic coast under Roman rule.

beats.scene: Roman soldiers rush out of a mountain town's gates at dawn
beats.summary: Galba's legion at Octodurus in the Alps is surrounded by Gauls, but it breaks out and wins.

beats.scene: Two Roman officers are held by Gauls on a quiet river bank
beats.summary: The Veneti seize Roman officers sent for grain, and Caesar orders a fleet built on the Loire.

beats.scene: A walled town on a rocky headland stands in the sea at high tide
beats.summary: The Veneti live in towns on headlands that the tide protects, and they sail away from each siege.

beats.scene: Huge oak ships with brown leather sails sit in a rocky harbour
beats.summary: The Veneti ships are thick oak with leather sails, much stronger than Roman ships.

beats.scene: Roman sailors with long hooks pull down the sails of an enemy ship
beats.summary: Brutus's sailors cut the ropes of the Veneti sails with hooks on long poles.

beats.scene: Dozens of becalmed ships lie on a flat sea under a bright sun
beats.summary: The wind drops, the Veneti cannot flee, and the Romans win the battle by sunset.

beats.scene: Caesar sits stern in a chair as Veneti nobles are led before him
beats.summary: Caesar punishes the Veneti harshly to teach respect for envoys.

beats.scene: German families with wagons and horses wait on the bank of a wide river
beats.summary: The Usipetes and Tencteri, driven out by the Suebi, cross the Rhine into Gaul.

beats.scene: German horsemen leap down and stab Roman horses from underneath
beats.summary: During a truce, eight hundred German horsemen beat five thousand Roman and Gallic cavalry.

beats.scene: German leaders stand under guard in a Roman camp at dawn
beats.summary: Caesar arrests the German leaders and marches against their army.

beats.scene: Roman cavalry chase fleeing German families toward a river junction
beats.summary: The leaderless Germans are routed, and many die at the junction of the Meuse and the Rhine.

beats.scene: A senator in a plain toga speaks angrily in a crowded Roman hall
beats.summary: Cato wants Caesar handed over, while Caesar decides to cross the Rhine.

beats.scene: Engineers lower great pointed beams into a wide swift river
beats.summary: Caesar's engineers begin a bridge over the Rhine, driving pairs of beams into the river bed.

beats.scene: A finished wooden bridge crosses a river with a line of piles upstream
beats.summary: The bridge is finished in ten days, with piles upstream to guard it.

beats.scene: A Roman army marches over a wooden bridge toward a dark forest
beats.summary: The Romans cross, and the Sugambri hide in the forests while their farms burn.

beats.scene: Roman soldiers break the planks of a wooden bridge behind them
beats.summary: After eighteen days in Germany, Caesar returns to Gaul and cuts the bridge.

beats.scene: A single Roman ship sails along high white cliffs scouting
beats.summary: Caesar decides to cross to Britain, and Volusenus scouts the coast for five days.

beats.scene: Roman ships with oars and sails approach tall white cliffs lined with warriors
beats.summary: Caesar sails with two legions and reaches the cliffs of Britain, with armed Britons on every height.

beats.scene: A fleet of Roman ships rows along a coast toward a flat open beach
beats.summary: Caesar waits until the afternoon, then sails seven miles to an open beach while the Britons follow.

beats.scene: Heavily armed soldiers hesitate on a ship's side above deep water
beats.summary: The ships cannot reach the beach, and the soldiers hesitate to jump into deep water.

beats.scene: A standard-bearer holding a golden eagle leaps from a ship into the waves
beats.summary: The standard-bearer of the tenth legion jumps into the sea, and the Romans follow.

beats.scene: Roman soldiers wade ashore as small boats row to help them
beats.summary: The beach fight is confused, but boats bring fresh soldiers and the Romans win the ground.

beats.scene: British envoys bring a chained man to Caesar's tent
beats.summary: The Britons ask for peace and return Commius, and a few hostages are given.

beats.scene: Broken Roman ships lie on a stormy beach under a full moon
beats.summary: A storm drives back the cavalry ships, and a high tide wrecks many Roman ships.

beats.scene: Roman sailors repair ships on a beach with wood and bronze from wrecks
beats.summary: The Britons plot to wait for winter, but Caesar repairs all but twelve ships.

beats.scene: British chariots race around Roman soldiers in a field of grain
beats.summary: The Britons ambush the seventh legion, and Caesar sees their chariot fighting for the first time.

beats.scene: Roman ships sail home across a grey sea at the end of summer
beats.summary: Caesar sails back to Gaul near the equinox, and Rome orders twenty days of thanks.

beats.scene: Hundreds of low wide ships stand on a muddy shore beside busy soldiers
beats.summary: In the winter of 55 to 54 BC, Caesar has his legions build a fleet of low, wide ships.

beats.scene: Roman cavalry ride into a Gallic village as chiefs hand over hostages
beats.summary: Caesar marches into the land of the Treveri and takes hostages from their leading families.

beats.scene: A Gallic noble rides hard with a sword raised as Roman horsemen chase him
beats.summary: Dumnorix refuses to sail with Caesar, rides away and dies fighting.

beats.scene: Hundreds of ships fill a calm sea at dawn as soldiers row
beats.summary: Five legions and two thousand cavalry cross to Britain in about eight hundred ships.

beats.scene: Roman soldiers climb an earth ramp into a woodland fort
beats.summary: The Romans land unopposed, march by night, and take a British stronghold.

beats.scene: Broken Roman ships lie on a stormy beach as men drag others ashore
beats.summary: A storm wrecks about forty ships, and Caesar hauls the rest inside a great fort.

beats.scene: British chiefs stand in a circle and hand a staff to one man
beats.summary: The Britons choose Cassivellaunus to lead them all.

beats.scene: British chariots race across a field around marching Roman soldiers
beats.summary: Cassivellaunus fights with chariots and fast raids, and the Romans struggle to pin him down.

beats.scene: Roman soldiers wade across a river with only their heads above water
beats.summary: Caesar crosses the Thames at its one ford, past stakes in the river bed.

beats.scene: A young British prince kneels before Caesar in a tent
beats.summary: The Trinovantes ask Caesar to protect Prince Mandubracius and offer to obey him.

beats.scene: British warriors flee through the back of a forest fort full of cattle
beats.summary: More tribes surrender and show Caesar the stronghold of Cassivellaunus, which falls.

beats.scene: Four British kings lead warriors toward a seaside Roman camp
beats.summary: Cassivellaunus orders the four kings of Kent to attack the Roman ships, and they fail.

beats.scene: A British king and Caesar speak as Commius translates in a tent
beats.summary: Cassivellaunus asks for peace, and Caesar demands hostages and a yearly payment.

beats.scene: Roman ships sail home with British captives under a pale sky
beats.summary: Caesar sails back to Gaul without leaving a garrison, and Cicero doubts the profit.

beats.scene: British warriors with blue painted bodies and long hair stand by a hut
beats.summary: Caesar describes the Britons, though much of it is hearsay.

beats.scene: Roman soldiers build winter huts in a dry brown Gallic landscape
beats.summary: A poor harvest makes Caesar spread his legions across Gaul in many camps.

beats.scene: Gauls attack Roman woodcutters at the edge of a forest
beats.summary: Ambiorix attacks the camp of Sabinus and Cotta and fails.

beats.scene: Ambiorix speaks earnestly to two Roman officers beside a river
beats.summary: Ambiorix tells the Romans that all Gaul will rise and offers them safe passage.

beats.scene: Roman officers argue loudly by lamplight in a tent at night
beats.summary: Cotta and Sabinus argue all night about whether to leave the camp.

beats.scene: A long Roman column winds down a deep wooded valley as Gauls watch
beats.summary: The Roman column marches into a deep valley, and Ambiorix's men attack.

beats.scene: Roman officers are surrounded by Gauls on a grassy field during a parley
beats.summary: Sabinus goes to talk with Ambiorix and is killed, and Cotta dies fighting.

beats.scene: A Gallic chief on a horse speaks to Nervian warriors by firelight
beats.summary: The last Romans die in the night, and Ambiorix rouses the Nervii against Quintus Cicero.

beats.scene: A sick Roman officer on a wall refuses an offer from a Gallic chief
beats.summary: The Nervii attack Cicero's camp and then ask him to talk, and Cicero refuses.

beats.scene: Roman soldiers raise tall wooden towers on a camp wall by torchlight
beats.summary: Cicero's soldiers build a hundred and twenty towers in a single night.

beats.scene: Burning Roman huts glow behind soldiers on a wall as sparks fly
beats.summary: The Nervii copy Roman siege methods and set the straw roofs on fire.

beats.scene: Two Roman centurions fight side by side outside a camp wall
beats.summary: The centurions Pullo and Vorenus rival each other in courage.

beats.scene: A Gallic slave slips through a crowd of besiegers with a hidden letter
beats.summary: Vertico's slave carries Cicero's letter through the enemy to Caesar.

beats.scene: Caesar leads a small Roman column across a wide valley at dawn
beats.summary: Caesar marches to help Cicero with only two legions.

beats.scene: A javelin with a leather strap sticks in a camp tower
beats.summary: Caesar fools the Gauls with a tiny camp and sends a letter by javelin.

beats.scene: Roman soldiers pour out of every gate of a small camp
beats.summary: The Gauls attack Caesar's small camp and are beaten, and Cicero's camp is saved.

beats.scene: Roman horsemen charge out of a camp gate toward a Gallic chief
beats.summary: Labienus pretends to be afraid, and his hidden cavalry kill Indutiomarus.

beats.scene: Fresh recruits in new armour line up in a Roman camp
beats.summary: Caesar raises three new legions, one lent by Pompey, and punishes the Nervii.

beats.scene: A second wooden bridge stands beside the first over a wide river
beats.summary: Caesar bridges the Rhine a second time, and the Suebi hide in a forest.

beats.scene: Gallic knights ride past bent farm workers in a field
beats.summary: Caesar describes the Gauls, who honour only the Druids and the knights.

beats.scene: A white-robed Druid leads young men reciting verses beneath old oaks
beats.summary: The Druids judge, teach for twenty years, and never write their lessons down.

beats.scene: Gauls gather beside a stone statue of a god with offerings
beats.summary: The Gauls honour many gods, which Caesar names for Roman ones.

beats.scene: German hunters walk through a vast pine forest at dawn
beats.summary: Caesar describes the Germans, who hunt and fight and own no fixed land.

beats.scene: A huge elk stands among tall trees in a dark ancient forest
beats.summary: Caesar describes the Hercynian Forest and its strange animals.

beats.scene: Roman soldiers burn farms while a Gallic chief escapes through a marsh
beats.summary: Caesar punishes the Eburones, but Ambiorix escapes again and again.

beats.scene: German horsemen gallop toward a Roman camp as sick soldiers grab spears
beats.summary: The Sugambri nearly capture the camp at Atuatuca, and Caesar blames Fortune.

beats.scene: Gallic chiefs whisper together at night in a dark forest clearing
beats.summary: In 52 BC, with Rome in turmoil, the Gauls plan a revolt in secret meetings.

beats.scene: Smoke rises over a Gallic town as Roman traders flee
beats.summary: The Carnutes kill the Roman traders at Cenabum, and the news is shouted across Gaul.

beats.scene: A young Gallic noble raises a sword before a cheering crowd
beats.summary: Vercingetorix, son of a murdered would-be king, is proclaimed king of the Arverni.

beats.scene: Gallic horsemen and spearmen gather beneath their chief's banner
beats.summary: Vercingetorix demands soldiers and hostages, and many peoples give him command.

beats.scene: Caesar studies a map in a tent with worried officers
beats.summary: Caesar must reach his scattered legions, so he hurries to defend the Province first.

beats.scene: Roman soldiers dig a path through deep snow in a mountain pass
beats.summary: Caesar crosses the snowy Cevennes and draws Vercingetorix back to defend his land.

beats.scene: A young Gallic chief addresses a council beneath a great tree
beats.summary: Vercingetorix proposes burning the countryside to starve the Romans.

beats.scene: Burning farms and villages light the Gallic horizon at dusk
beats.summary: The Bituriges burn twenty towns in a day, but beg to save Avaricum.

beats.scene: Roman soldiers rush through the gates of a burning walled town at night
beats.summary: Caesar takes Cenabum and burns it, and he marches into the land of the Bituriges.

beats.scene: Hungry Roman soldiers roast meat over fires beside a walled town
beats.summary: At Avaricum the Roman soldiers go without bread and refuse to give up the siege.

beats.scene: A walled town on a rise almost circled by a river and marshes
beats.summary: Avaricum is nearly surrounded by water, and its wall of timber and stone resists fire and rams.

beats.scene: Roman soldiers pile earth and timber into a huge ramp beside a town wall
beats.summary: The Romans build a ramp three hundred and thirty feet wide and eighty feet high.

beats.scene: Gallic miners dig tunnels beneath a Roman ramp as fire flickers above
beats.summary: The Gauls tunnel under the ramp and use hooks and fire against the Roman works.

beats.scene: A Gaul on a town wall hands flaming pitch to his friends
beats.summary: A Gaul keeps the fire coming until a Roman bolt strikes him, and another takes his place.

beats.scene: Heavy rain falls on a wall as guards shelter and Roman soldiers wait
beats.summary: On a rainy day Caesar sees that the guards on the wall are careless and plans an attack.

beats.scene: Roman soldiers swarm up a ramp and over a town wall
beats.summary: At a signal the Romans rush the wall and drive the Gauls out of Avaricum.

beats.scene: Crowds of people jam the gates of a town as Roman soldiers pour in
beats.summary: The soldiers spare nobody, and only about eight hundred people escape from forty thousand.

beats.scene: Vercingetorix speaks calmly to a crowd of Gauls in his camp
beats.summary: Vercingetorix says that the loss was not his fault, and Gaul trusts him more.

beats.scene: Caesar listens to two Gallic nobles arguing in a council tent
beats.summary: Caesar settles a quarrel of the Aedui and divides his army between himself and Labienus.

beats.scene: Roman soldiers rebuild a bridge beneath a wood at dusk
beats.summary: Caesar tricks Vercingetorix with hidden legions, rebuilds a bridge and crosses the river.

beats.scene: A town crowns a steep mountain as Roman soldiers climb a small hill
beats.summary: Caesar sees that Gergovia cannot be stormed, so he takes a small hill beside it.

beats.scene: A young noble in tears addresses a column of marching soldiers
beats.summary: Litaviccus tells ten thousand Aeduan soldiers a false story that Caesar has killed their leaders.

beats.scene: Two Gallic nobles ride before astonished soldiers while Roman cavalry watch
beats.summary: Caesar marches through the night and shows the Aedui that their leaders are alive.

beats.scene: Muleteers in helmets ride along a ridge as soldiers creep up a slope
beats.summary: Caesar finds one side of Gergovia thinly guarded and plans a surprise.

beats.scene: Roman soldiers rush into an empty hillside camp as a half-dressed king flees
beats.summary: The Romans capture three Gallic camps, but they ignore the signal to stop.

beats.scene: Women on a town wall throw clothes and silver and hold out their hands
beats.summary: Gaulish women plead for mercy from the wall, and some Romans climb up.

beats.scene: A Roman centurion fights alone at a town gate as his men retreat
beats.summary: The centurion Petronius gives his life to save his soldiers.

beats.scene: Roman soldiers climb a steep slope as Gauls pour out of the town above
beats.summary: The Gauls counterattack, and the Romans lose forty-six centurions.

beats.scene: Caesar speaks sternly to rows of ashamed soldiers in camp
beats.summary: Caesar scolds the soldiers for ignoring orders, though he praises their courage.

beats.scene: Roman baggage burns in a Gallic town as an army wades a flooded river
beats.summary: The Aedui rebel and burn Noviodunum, and Caesar crosses the flooded Loire.

beats.scene: A Roman column marches along a river toward an island town beyond a marsh
beats.summary: Labienus marches toward Lutetia but cannot cross the marsh that Camulogenus holds.

beats.scene: Roman soldiers climb into a fleet of captured boats by moonlight
beats.summary: Labienus takes fifty boats and the town of Metiosedum without a fight.

beats.scene: Gauls burn a bridge and a town on a river island
beats.summary: Camulogenus burns Lutetia, and Labienus hears of Gergovia and the Aeduan revolt.

beats.scene: Roman soldiers row quietly across a dark river as noise rises upstream
beats.summary: Labienus fools the Gauls with a noisy false march and crosses the Seine unseen.

beats.scene: Roman soldiers and Gauls fight on a river bank as an old chief falls
beats.summary: Labienus wins the battle, Camulogenus dies, and Labienus rejoins Caesar.

beats.scene: Gallic chiefs gather in a great circle around a young leader
beats.summary: At Bibracte the Gauls confirm Vercingetorix as leader of the whole war.

beats.scene: German horsemen on small horses arrive at a Roman camp
beats.summary: Caesar brings German horsemen across the Rhine and heads toward the Province.

beats.scene: German cavalry gallop up a ridge to drive off Gallic horsemen
beats.summary: Vercingetorix attacks with his cavalry, but the Germans win the ridge and the day.

beats.scene: A beaten Gallic army marches toward a hill town as Roman riders follow
beats.summary: Vercingetorix retreats to Alesia, and Caesar follows and camps nearby.

beats.scene: A hill town stands above two rivers and a wide plain
beats.summary: Caesar studies Alesia, a town on a lofty hill between two rivers.

beats.scene: A column of Gallic horsemen rides out of a hill town gate at night
beats.summary: Vercingetorix sends his cavalry away to bring help and puts his grain on strict rations.

beats.scene: Gallic and German cavalry clash on a wide plain below a hill town
beats.summary: Caesar decides to starve Alesia out, after a cavalry fight won by the Germans.

beats.scene: Roman soldiers dig a deep ditch and build a wall around a hill town
beats.summary: The inner Roman line runs eleven miles, with twenty-three forts, ditches and a rampart.

beats.scene: Sharpened stakes and hidden pits fill a field in front of a Roman wall
beats.summary: The Romans plant tombstones, lilies and goads, traps that wound anyone who charges.

beats.scene: A second Roman wall faces outward across open country
beats.summary: Caesar builds an outer line fourteen miles long and stores grain for thirty days.

beats.scene: Gallic chiefs around a table assign groups of warriors to each tribe
beats.summary: The Gauls call a relief army of two hundred and fifty thousand foot soldiers and eight thousand horsemen.

beats.scene: Gallic leaders in a besieged town argue around an almost empty grain store
beats.summary: The day for help passes, and the people of Alesia run short of grain.

beats.scene: A tall Gallic noble speaks fiercely at a council inside a hill town
beats.summary: Critognatus argues against surrender and recalls the Gauls' war with the Cimbri.

beats.scene: Families leave a hill town through a gate, carrying bundles
beats.summary: The Mandubii and their families are driven out of Alesia to save food.

beats.scene: Hungry women and children stand outside a Roman wall begging for bread
beats.summary: Caesar refuses to feed the Mandubii, and they are left between the lines.

beats.scene: A vast Gallic army appears on distant hills as people cheer
beats.summary: The Gaulish relief army arrives, and Alesia cheers.

beats.scene: Gallic and German cavalry fight on a plain while onlookers crowd a town wall
beats.summary: On the first day the German cavalry beat the Gaulish cavalry and archers on the plain.

beats.scene: Gauls with ladders and hooks creep toward a Roman rampart at midnight
beats.summary: The Gauls attack at midnight, and Antony and Trebonius throw them back.

beats.scene: Gallic scouts study a Roman camp on a hillside from a ridge
beats.summary: The Gauls find a weak spot on the northern hill and choose sixty thousand picked men.

beats.scene: A great Gallic army moves down a hillside at noon toward a Roman camp
beats.summary: At noon the Gauls attack from the hill, from the plain and from Alesia at once.

beats.scene: Roman defenders on a tower hurl stones as arrows fly in both directions
beats.summary: The Romans are pressed on every side, and Caesar watches from a high place.

beats.scene: Gauls cover a ditch with earth and wicker as tired Romans hold a wall
beats.summary: On the northern hill the Gauls fill the ditches, and the Romans run short of missiles.

beats.scene: Caesar in a bright cloak leads fresh soldiers down a hill to battle
beats.summary: Caesar arrives himself with fresh troops, and the Romans cheer.

beats.scene: Roman cohorts break out of a fort as cavalry rides around the Gauls' rear
beats.summary: Labienus and Caesar attack from the front while the cavalry strikes from behind.

beats.scene: Gallic warriors flee across a plain as Roman riders chase them
beats.summary: The Gaulish army breaks and flees, and Vercingetorix withdraws into Alesia.

beats.scene: A tall Gallic chief lays down his weapons before Caesar's seat
beats.summary: Vercingetorix offers himself to save his people, and Alesia surrenders.

beats.scene: Roman soldiers lead long lines of prisoners away from a ruined siege camp
beats.summary: Caesar sets aside the Aedui and Arverni prisoners, gives the rest to his soldiers, and Rome gives thanks.

beats.scene: Roman and Gallic soldiers face each other beside a wood in autumn
beats.summary: In 51 BC the Bellovaci rise, and Caesar's officer Hirtius tells the last campaigns.

beats.scene: Roman engineers dig a tunnel under a spring beside a hill fortress
beats.summary: Uxellodunum falls when Caesar's engineers cut off its spring.

beats.scene: Caesar rides through a peaceful Gallic village in the sun
beats.summary: Hirtius says that Caesar spent his last year in Gaul keeping the peace gently.

beats.scene: Vercingetorix stands in chains in a Roman parade
beats.summary: Vercingetorix is held in Rome for about six years and led in Caesar's triumph in 46 BC.

beats.scene: A general leads his soldiers across a small river at dawn
beats.summary: Caesar crosses the Rubicon in 49 BC, wins the civil war, and is murdered in 44 BC.

beats.scene: Caesar dictates to a scribe who writes on a wax tablet
beats.summary: Caesar wrote the account himself, so readers must remember that it is only his side.

beats.scene: Diggers measure old ditches on a green hillside
beats.summary: Caesar's numbers are doubtful, but digging at Alesia matches his description.

beats.scene: A Roman road runs straight through green fields of Gaul
beats.summary: Gaul becomes Roman, and its language and law slowly change.

A1A2: Caesar wrote that all of Gaul was divided into three parts.
The northern people, the Belgae, lived far from Roman towns and were very brave.
A rich man named Orgetorix told his people to leave their small land.
For two years the Helvetii built wagons and saved grain for the journey.
Someone told the Helvetii about the plot, and Orgetorix had to face a trial.
The Helvetii burned their own homes so that nobody wanted to come back.
The Romans later found a list of names that counted three hundred and sixty-eight thousand people.
The Helvetii wanted the shorter road, which went through the Roman land.
In Rome, Caesar heard that the Helvetii were already on the move.
Caesar left Rome quickly and rode to Gaul with only one legion there.
Caesar cut the bridge at Geneva, then told the Helvetii to wait.
His soldiers built a long wall and a deep ditch along the river.
The Helvetii tried to cross the river, but the Romans stopped them.
Dumnorix asked the Sequani to let the Helvetii use the mountain road.
Caesar went to Italy, called more soldiers, and came back with five legions.
The Helvetii ruined the Aedui fields, so the Aedui asked Caesar for help.
At night Caesar's soldiers attacked the men still waiting on the river bank.
Caesar built a bridge over the river in a single day.
Divico said that the Helvetii would go anywhere Caesar wished, if there was peace.
Caesar wanted hostages, but Divico said his people never gave any.
Caesar's horsemen rode ahead, but five hundred Helvetian riders beat them.
For fifteen days Caesar followed the Helvetii, but he ran short of grain.
Liscus, an Aeduan chief, told Caesar that Dumnorix was blocking the grain.
Caesar did not punish Dumnorix, because his brother Diviciacus cried and begged.
Labienus took the hill, but a scout wrongly said it was full of Gauls.
With only two days of grain left, Caesar turned toward Bibracte.
Caesar sent away all the horses, so that no man could run.
The Romans threw spears from the hill and broke the Helvetian shield wall.
Then two more tribes attacked the Romans from the side.
The Helvetii fought behind their wagons until night, then they ran away.
The Helvetii gave up and went home to rebuild their towns.
Chiefs from all over Gaul came to thank Caesar for his victory.
The Germans had crossed the Rhine, and their king, Ariovistus, was cruel.
Only the Sequani said nothing, and they looked at the ground.
Ariovistus said that Caesar should visit him if he wanted anything.
Caesar marched fast and took the great town of Vesontio.
Roman soldiers heard that the Germans were huge, and they were afraid.
Caesar called the officers together and told them they should be ashamed.
The tenth legion thanked Caesar, and the whole army marched out.
Ariovistus asked for a talk, and Caesar agreed to meet him.
The two leaders met on a mound, but the talk went badly.
Ariovistus put a Roman messenger in chains, and Caesar was angry.
The German women said not to fight before the new moon.
The Romans ran so fast that the Germans could not throw spears.
Young Crassus saw the danger and sent soldiers to help the left side.
Ariovistus found a small boat and escaped across the Rhine.
Caesar found Procillus alive, and he was happier than after the victory.
Caesar put his army in winter camps and went to northern Italy.
News came that the Belgae were making plans to fight the Romans.
The Remi joined Rome, and Caesar sent archers to save their town.
Caesar made camp beside the river, and the Belgae could not cross.
The Belgae argued, then each tribe went home in the night.
The Suessiones saw the Roman towers and soon gave up.
The Nervii were the strongest Belgae, and they would not drink wine.
Suddenly the Nervii ran out of the trees and attacked the Romans.
Caesar had to give every order at the same moment.
Caesar took a shield and ran to the front to fight.
The left wing drove the Atrebates back into the river.
The Nervii climbed over their own dead and kept fighting.
Of six hundred Nervian leaders, only three were left alive.
The Atuatuci laughed at the Roman tower, then they gave up.
The Atuatuci hid some weapons and attacked the Romans in the night.
Rome held fifteen days of thanks, and nobody had ever had so many.
In the Alps, Gauls from the hills attacked Galba's winter camp.
The Veneti caught two Roman officers and would not let them go.
The Veneti lived in towns on cliffs that the sea cut off.
Veneti ships were made of strong oak and had sails of leather.
Roman sailors used long hooks to cut the ropes of the sails.
The wind died, and the Veneti ships could not escape.
After the battle, Caesar punished the Veneti and sold many as slaves.
Two German peoples crossed the Rhine, because other Germans chased them.
German riders attacked during the truce, and the Romans lost many men.
The next day, Caesar held the German leaders and attacked their camp.
The Germans ran away to the river, and many of them died.
Cato wanted Rome to hand Caesar over to the Germans.
Caesar's engineers began to build a bridge over the Rhine.
Ten days after the first log, the bridge was ready.
The army crossed the bridge, and the Sugambri ran into the forests.
Caesar stayed in Germany for eighteen days, then he went home.
Caesar wanted to see Britain, so he sent a scout ahead.
Caesar sailed with two legions, and they reached Britain in the morning.
Caesar waited for his ships, then sailed along the coast to find a beach.
The water was deep, and the soldiers were afraid to jump down.
The eagle-bearer jumped into the sea, and the soldiers followed him.
The fight was hard, because the soldiers could not keep their lines.
The Britons asked for peace and promised to give hostages.
A storm came, and the sea broke many of the Roman ships.
Caesar's men repaired the damaged ships using wood from the broken ones.
The Britons attacked the seventh legion, but Caesar came to help.
Caesar sailed home after the summer, and Rome gave twenty days of thanks.
Caesar ordered many new ships, wide and low, for the sea.
Caesar went to the Treveri, and their chiefs promised to obey him.
Dumnorix tried to escape, but Caesar's horsemen caught and killed him.
Eight hundred ships crossed the sea, and no enemy stopped them.
The Britons saw all the ships and ran to the hills.
A storm wrecked many ships, so Caesar went back to the shore.
The Britons chose a new war leader named Cassivellaunus.
Fast British carts pulled by horses made the Romans' fight very hard.
Caesar's army crossed the Thames at its only shallow place.
The Trinovantes asked Caesar to protect their young prince.
Many British tribes gave up and showed Caesar the way to the fort.
Four kings attacked the Roman ships, but the Romans beat them.
Cassivellaunus asked for peace, and Caesar named his terms.
Caesar sailed home with prisoners, but he left no soldiers there.
Many Britons painted their bodies blue and wore their hair long.
The harvest was poor, so Caesar put his army in many camps.
Ambiorix's men attacked Romans cutting wood, then they attacked the camp.
Ambiorix said that all Gaul would rise, and the Romans should leave.
Cotta said not to trust an enemy, but Sabinus wanted to leave.
The Romans marched out, and the Gauls attacked them in a valley.
Sabinus went to talk with Ambiorix, and the Gauls killed him.
Ambiorix told other tribes that the Romans could be beaten.
Cicero was ill, but he refused to talk with his enemies.
The Romans built one hundred and twenty towers in a single night.
The Gauls threw fire onto the roofs of the Roman huts.
Two centurions, Pullo and Vorenus, each wanted to be the best.
A slave carried Cicero's letter through the Gauls and reached Caesar.
Caesar got the letter and marched at once with two legions.
Caesar made his camp very small to make the Gauls think he was afraid.
The Gauls attacked Caesar's small camp, and the Romans beat them.
Labienus pretended to be afraid, and his horsemen killed Indutiomarus.
Caesar raised three new legions, and Pompey lent him one.
Caesar built another bridge over the Rhine, and the Suebi hid.
Only priests and noble riders had power among the Gauls.
Druids taught young men songs for twenty years and wrote nothing down.
The Gauls honoured many gods, and Mercury was the most important.
The Germans lived by hunting and war, and owned little land.
A huge German forest took nine days to cross.
Caesar hunted Ambiorix, but the Eburones chief always escaped him.
German riders nearly took a Roman camp while the soldiers were away.
Rome was in disorder, so the Gauls thought Caesar could not leave Italy.
The Carnutes killed the Romans at Cenabum, and the news spread quickly.
Vercingetorix, a young Arvernian, raised an army and made himself king.
Vercingetorix told every tribe to send soldiers, and many agreed.
Caesar rushed north and went to protect the Roman land.
Caesar crossed the snowy mountains and surprised the Arverni.
Vercingetorix told the Gauls to burn farms so the Romans would starve.
The Bituriges burned twenty towns, but they begged to keep Avaricum.
Caesar burned Cenabum to punish the Carnutes for killing Romans.
The Roman soldiers had no grain, but they did not complain.
Avaricum had a river and a marsh around it, with one narrow way in.
The Romans piled up a huge ramp of earth beside the wall.
The Gauls dug tunnels under the ramp and set it on fire.
One Gaul kept throwing fire until a Roman bolt hit him.
Heavy rain fell, and the Gauls on the wall grew careless.
At a signal the Romans ran up the ramp and over the wall.
The Romans took Avaricum, and only eight hundred people escaped.
Vercingetorix told the Gauls that the defeat was not his fault.
Caesar settled a quarrel among the Aedui and then divided his army.
Caesar tricked Vercingetorix and crossed the river on a bridge.
Gergovia stood on a very high hill, and it was hard to reach.
Litaviccus told the Aedui soldiers a lie about Caesar.
Caesar marched all night and showed the Aedui that the lie was false.
Caesar went back to Gergovia and saw a way to attack.
The soldiers took three Gaulish camps and then ran on to the wall.
Women on the wall begged the Romans not to hurt them.
A brave centurion, Marcus Petronius, fought to save his men and died.
Forty-six centurions died on the slope that day.
Caesar spoke angrily to the soldiers for ignoring his order to stop.
Then the Aedui turned against Caesar and joined Vercingetorix.
Labienus marched toward Lutetia, but a big marsh stopped him.
Labienus changed his plan and took fifty boats at Metiosedum.
Camulogenus burned Lutetia and its bridges, and Labienus was in danger.
Labienus made much noise upstream to trick the Gauls at night.
The Romans won the battle, and Camulogenus died fighting.
The Gauls met at Bibracte, and again chose Vercingetorix as their leader.
Caesar called for German horsemen, because he had lost his Gallic riders.
Vercingetorix attacked with his horsemen, but the German riders beat him.
After this defeat, Vercingetorix led his army to the town of Alesia.
Alesia stood on a hill with two rivers and steep slopes.
Vercingetorix sent his horsemen away to bring more Gauls to help.
Caesar decided to starve the Gauls instead of storming the hill.
The Romans built a wall eleven miles long around the hill.
The Romans hid sharp stakes in holes to stop the Gauls.
The Romans built a second wall, facing outward, fourteen miles long.
All over Gaul, the tribes sent men to help Vercingetorix.
Inside Alesia, the Gauls counted the days, but no help came.
Critognatus said that the Gauls must never give up, whatever the cost.
The Gauls decided to send the women and children out of Alesia.
The Mandubii begged the Romans for food, but Caesar said no.
A huge Gaulish army arrived, and the people in Alesia cheered.
On the first day, Gaulish riders attacked, but the German cavalry beat them.
At midnight, the Gauls attacked the wall with ladders and hooks.
The Gauls looked for a weak place in the Roman wall.
At noon the Gauls attacked from all sides at once.
The Romans fought on both walls, and the Gauls pressed hard.
The Gauls on the northern hill nearly broke the Roman camp.
Caesar came in his general's cloak, and the soldiers shouted for joy.
Caesar and Labienus attacked the Gauls from the front and the back.
The Gauls ran away, and many were killed or caught.
Vercingetorix gave himself up, and the Gauls laid down their weapons.
Caesar gave each soldier a prisoner, except the Aedui and Arverni.
A year later, the last Gauls rebelled, and Caesar's officers fought them.
At Uxellodunum, the Romans cut off the spring, and the town gave up.
After the war, Caesar treated the Gauls gently and kept the peace.
Vercingetorix was held in Rome for six years, then killed.
Caesar led his army into Italy, and a civil war began.
Caesar wrote the book himself, so it shows only his side.
People dug up the old Roman ditches at Alesia many years later.
Gaul became a Roman land, and the people slowly learned Latin.
B1B2: Caesar begins his book by saying that Gaul is divided into three parts. One part is home to the Belgae, one to the Aquitani, and one to the people who call themselves Celts.
The Belgae in the north, Caesar says, are the bravest of all the Gauls. They live farthest from the Roman Province, so merchants rarely bring them the soft comforts that weaken a people.
The richest man among the Helvetii is a noble named Orgetorix. He tells his people that they are hemmed in by mountains, a lake and the Rhine, and that they deserve a bigger land.
The Helvetii agree and spend two years buying wagons, animals and grain. Meanwhile Orgetorix secretly persuades two other nobles, Casticus and Dumnorix, to help him take power in their own peoples.

Somebody betrays the plot, and the Helvetii order Orgetorix to answer for it in chains. He arrives with ten thousand followers, but he dies before the trial is over, and some suspect that he killed himself.
The Helvetii do not give up the plan after his death. They burn twelve towns, about four hundred villages and all the grain they cannot carry, so that no one will want to turn back.
Neighbouring peoples join the march, and the Romans later find a list written in Greek letters. It counts three hundred and sixty-eight thousand people, though Caesar's numbers are often too large.
There are two roads out of the Helvetian land, and one of them is much shorter. It runs through the Roman Province beside the Rhône, so Caesar knows that the Helvetii are heading straight for him.
Caesar is still near Rome when the news arrives, and he is alarmed. He understands at once that a whole people on the move would be a danger to the Roman Province, and he does not wait.
Caesar leaves the city and travels to Further Gaul as fast as he can. He finds only one legion there, so he sends orders to raise as many soldiers as possible.
At Geneva, Caesar orders the bridge over the Rhône to be cut down. When envoys ask to cross the Province peacefully, he says he must think, and tells them to come back in two weeks.

The soldiers build a wall sixteen feet high along the Roman bank of the Rhône, with a deep ditch in front of it. It runs for nearly nineteen miles from Lake Geneva to the Jura mountains, and forts stand along it at short distances.

When the Helvetii return, Caesar tells them that Roman custom does not allow any army to pass through the Province. They try to cross by boat and at shallow places, by day and by night, but Roman missiles drive them back each time.

The Helvetii now turn to the other road, through the narrow mountain pass of the Sequani. Dumnorix, who is popular among the Sequani, arranges that the two peoples will give each other hostages and that the Helvetii will cross in peace.

Caesar learns that the Helvetii mean to march west toward the land of the Santones, close to the Province. He leaves Labienus in charge of the wall, hurries to Italy, raises two legions, and returns over the Alps with five.
Meanwhile the Helvetii have crossed the land of the Sequani and are ruining the fields of the Aedui. The Aedui, who are friends of Rome, send messengers to ask Caesar to protect them.
At night Caesar leads three legions against the Helvetii still waiting on the near bank of the Saône. Three quarters of the people have already crossed, and most of those left behind are cut down.

Caesar then builds a bridge over the Saône in one day, although the Helvetii needed twenty days to cross it on rafts. The Helvetii are astonished, and they send an old chief named Divico to ask for peace.
Divico says that if Rome will make peace, the Helvetii will settle wherever Caesar chooses. If not, he warns, Caesar should remember the old Roman defeat and the courage of the Helvetii.

Caesar replies that he remembers the old defeat well, but he will make peace only if the Helvetii give hostages and repay the Aedui. Divico answers that his people are used to receiving hostages, not giving them, and he leaves.
Caesar sends four thousand horsemen ahead to see which way the Helvetii go. Only five hundred Helvetian riders meet them, yet they drive the Roman horsemen back, and the Helvetii grow bolder.
For about fifteen days the Roman army follows the Helvetii, staying five or six miles behind them. The Aedui have promised grain, but each day they find a new reason to delay.

At last Caesar calls Liscus, the chief magistrate of the Aedui, and presses him for the truth. Liscus admits, reluctantly, that Dumnorix is rich, popular and an enemy of Rome, and that he is stopping the grain on purpose.
Caesar then calls Diviciacus, the brother of Dumnorix and a loyal friend of Rome. Diviciacus weeps and begs Caesar not to punish his brother, so Caesar forgives Dumnorix but sets guards to watch him.

Caesar learns that the Helvetii are camped eight miles away, and he sends Labienus to take the hill above them. A scout named Considius swears that the hill is held by Gauls, so Caesar holds back and the chance is lost.

Caesar has only two days' grain left, so he turns toward the rich town of Bibracte, about eighteen miles away. A deserter tells the Helvetii, who think that the Romans are afraid, and they turn around to attack.
Caesar stops on a hill and sends his own horse away, then the horses of all his officers. Now everyone will face the same danger, and no one will be able to run away.
The Helvetii march up the slope in a tight mass, with their shields locked together. The Romans hurl their javelins from above, and many pierce two shields at once, pinning them together.

As the Romans push forward, the Boii and the Tulingi, who have been guarding the Helvetian rear, attack the open Roman flank. The Romans form two fronts, and the battle goes on from the early afternoon until night.

The Helvetii fight on behind their wagons, and even the women and children hurl spears and stones from above. Late at night the Romans take the camp, and about a hundred and thirty thousand Helvetii escape into the darkness.

Caesar waits three days, then the hungry Helvetii surrender and give hostages and weapons. He sends them home to rebuild their burnt towns, and the census shows only about a hundred and ten thousand people left.
Chiefs from nearly every state in Gaul come to congratulate Caesar. Then they ask to speak with him in secret, and when he agrees, they fall at his feet in tears.

Diviciacus explains that the Sequani invited fifteen thousand Germans across the Rhine to fight the Aedui. Now there are about a hundred and twenty thousand, and their king Ariovistus has taken a third of the Sequani's land and wants more.

Only the Sequani stay silent and stare at the ground, and Diviciacus says that they fear the cruelty of Ariovistus. Caesar decides to act, since Rome cannot let her friends the Aedui be ruined, and he asks Ariovistus for a meeting.

Ariovistus replies that if Caesar wants something, he must come himself, for the German king does not go to the Romans. Caesar then demands that no more Germans cross the Rhine, but Ariovistus answers that he rules by the right of war.

More bad news arrives, because the Harudes are plundering the Aedui, and the Suebi are gathering at the Rhine. Caesar marches fast and seizes Vesontio, the largest town of the Sequani, before Ariovistus can reach it.

While the army waits at Vesontio, traders tell wild stories about the Germans, who are huge and terrible in battle. Fear spreads from the young officers to the whole army, and some men make their wills or beg to go home.

Caesar calls the officers together and scolds them for doubting their general. He reminds them that Marius once beat the Germans, and swears to march with only the tenth legion if the rest are afraid.

The tenth legion thanks Caesar warmly, and the other legions are ashamed and say that they were never afraid. Caesar marches for seven days, and the scouts tell him that Ariovistus is only twenty-four miles away.
Ariovistus now asks for a meeting, and Caesar agrees. Because he distrusts the Gallic horsemen, he lets men of the tenth legion ride their horses instead.

Caesar and Ariovistus meet on a mound in an open plain, each with ten horsemen. Caesar reminds the king of Rome's favours, but Ariovistus answers proudly, and then his horsemen start throwing stones at the Romans.
Ariovistus asks for another meeting, but Caesar will not risk it, and he sends two envoys, Procillus and Mettius, instead. Ariovistus accuses them of spying and puts them in chains.
Prisoners tell Caesar that German wise women have forbidden Ariovistus to fight before the new moon. Caesar therefore attacks at once, and the Germans have to leave their camp and fight.

The Romans charge so fast that the Germans cannot throw their spears, and the two sides fight hand to hand. When the Germans lock their shields together, Roman soldiers leap onto them and tear the shields down.
Publius Crassus, the young commander of the cavalry, sees that the Roman left is in trouble. Without waiting for orders, he sends the third line to help, and the battle turns.
The Germans run toward the Rhine, about five miles away, and the Roman cavalry chase them. Ariovistus finds a small boat tied to the bank and escapes, but most of the others are caught and killed.

While chasing the enemy, Caesar finds Procillus, who is being dragged along in chains by his guards. Caesar is overjoyed, and Procillus says that the Germans three times drew lots to burn him, but each time he was spared.

The Suebi who had gathered on the Rhine go home in fear, and the campaign of 58 BC is over. Caesar puts the army into winter quarters, leaves Labienus in command, and goes to northern Italy to hold the law courts.

In northern Italy, Caesar hears from Labienus that the Belgae are plotting against Rome, fearing that they will be attacked next. He raises two new legions, and in early summer he marches north to meet them.

The Remi, the nearest of the Belgae, give hostages to Caesar and tell him that their cousins are gathering a huge army. When the Belgae attack their town of Bibrax, Caesar sends archers and slingers, and the attackers give up.
Caesar camps on a ridge beside the river Aisne, protects it with ditches and forts, and waits. The Belgae try to cross a ford in the marsh, but Roman archers and slingers drive them back.

Short of food, the Belgae agree to go home and to return to defend whichever tribe the Romans attack first. They leave at night in noisy disorder, and Caesar's cavalry catch the rearguard and cut it down the next day.
Caesar marches quickly into the land of the Suessiones and attacks their town of Noviodunum. The Gauls have never seen siege towers and ramps, and they are so amazed that they surrender at once.

The Nervii are the fiercest of the Belgae, and they refuse wine because they think it makes men soft. With their neighbours the Atrebates and the Viromandui, they plan to ambush the Romans on the march.

The Roman army reaches the river Sabis and begins to build a camp on the hill, with the baggage still coming up behind. Suddenly the Nervii burst out of the woods across the river, cross it in a moment, and fall on the Romans.

Caesar has to do everything at once: he raises the flag, sounds the trumpet, and calls back the men who are gathering wood. There is no time to put on helmets or to take the covers off the shields, so every soldier fights where he stands.
Caesar takes a shield from a soldier in the rear and pushes to the front, where the fighting is worst. He calls the centurions by name and shouts to the men to keep their courage.

On the left, the ninth and tenth legions drive the Atrebates back across the river. In the centre two other legions beat the Viromandui, but the Nervii pour through the open space on the right and surround the camp.
The Nervii in front fall in heaps, but those behind climb over the bodies and keep fighting. Labienus, who has taken the enemy camp, sees the danger and sends the tenth legion back to help.

Caesar says that the Nervii were almost wiped out: only three of their six hundred senators survived. Only about five hundred of their sixty thousand fighting men were left, and Caesar spared the old men, women and children.
The Atuatuci are descendants of the Cimbri and Teutones, and they hide in a strong town. They laugh at the small Romans for building a tower, but when it rolls toward the wall, they ask for peace.

The Atuatuci throw so many weapons from the wall that the pile is almost as high as the wall. But they have kept a third of their arms and attack that night, and Caesar sells all the survivors as slaves.

Meanwhile young Publius Crassus, with one legion, brings the tribes along the Atlantic coast under Roman rule. When Caesar's report reaches Rome, the Senate orders fifteen days of public thanksgiving, an honour that no general has ever received before.
Galba spends the winter with one legion in the Alps, in the mountain town of Octodurus. When the Gauls seize the hills around the town, the outnumbered Romans make a sudden attack and drive them off.
In the winter, young Crassus sends officers to the coastal tribes to ask for grain. The Veneti, the greatest sea power in the region, seize two of them and hope to swap them for their own hostages.

Veneti towns stand on headlands, and at high tide the sea surrounds them, so the Romans cannot walk to them. Caesar builds great earth banks against them, but each time the Veneti sail away with their people and goods.

The Veneti ships are built of thick oak, held together with iron nails, and their anchors hang on iron chains instead of ropes. Their sails are soft leather, and the lower Roman ships cannot damage them by ramming.

Decimus Brutus, who commands the Roman fleet, tells his sailors to fasten sharp hooks to long poles. They catch the ropes that hold the Veneti sails and row hard, and the yards fall so that the ships cannot move.
Then the wind drops completely, and the Veneti ships cannot move. Two or three Roman ships close round each enemy ship, and the battle lasts from about ten in the morning until sunset.
After the battle the Veneti surrender, and Caesar decides to punish them harshly. He puts the council to death and sells the rest as slaves, to teach everyone to respect envoys.

The Usipetes and Tencteri, pushed out of their land by the powerful Suebi, cross the Rhine into Gaul. Caesar, who knows how quickly the Gauls change sides, hurries north to the army before they can join the Germans.

Caesar tells the Germans to settle among the Ubii, and they ask for three days to think. During the truce eight hundred German horsemen charge five thousand Roman and Gallic cavalry and throw them into confusion.
Next morning the German leaders come to Caesar's camp to apologise for the attack. Caesar does not believe them, so he keeps them prisoner and marches at once against their leaderless army.
The Germans, taken by surprise, cannot find their weapons or their leaders. They run toward the place where the Rhine and the Meuse meet, and many are killed there, including women and children.

When the news reaches Rome, the senator Cato says that Caesar broke a truce and proposes to hand him over to the Germans. Caesar, for his part, decides to cross the Rhine, because the Ubii ask for help and he wants the Germans to fear Rome.

Caesar thinks that boats are neither safe nor worthy of Rome, so he orders his engineers to build a bridge. They drive pairs of heavy beams into the river bed, and then they lay long timbers across them.
Ten days after the timber is first brought to the river, the bridge is finished. To protect it from floating logs and boats, the Romans drive extra piles upstream and post guards at both ends.

The Roman army crosses the bridge, and the Sugambri, whose land is nearest, leave their homes and hide in the forests. Caesar burns their villages and farms, and the Ubii, who are friends of Rome, thank him.

Caesar decides that he has done enough to frighten the Germans, since the Suebi will not come out to fight. He spends eighteen days beyond the Rhine, returns to Gaul, and cuts down the bridge behind him.

Although summer is nearly over, Caesar decides to sail to Britain, because the Britons have often sent help to the Gauls. Traders can tell him nothing about the harbours, so he sends an officer named Volusenus in a warship to look.

Caesar sails around midnight with two legions on eighty transports, while eighteen more ships wait in another port for the cavalry. By mid-morning the ships reach the coast of Britain, where armed Britons crowd the high cliffs.

Caesar waits at anchor until three in the afternoon for the rest of his ships, and he briefs the officers. Then, with wind and tide in his favour, he sails about seven miles along the coast to an open, level beach.

The big ships cannot come close to the beach, so the soldiers must jump into deep water, carrying their heavy weapons. The Britons wait on dry land or wade out, and they hurl spears at men who cannot see where to put their feet.

Then the standard-bearer of the tenth legion calls to the others to jump, unless they want the enemy to take the eagle. He leaps into the water and carries the eagle toward the Britons, and the other soldiers, ashamed to stay behind, jump after him.

On the beach the fighting is confused, because the soldiers cannot find their own standards and the Britons attack them in small groups. Caesar fills the small boats with men and sends them where help is needed, and the Romans slowly gain the beach.

The Britons send envoys to ask for peace, and they bring back Commius, whom they had chained when he landed. Caesar scolds them, accepts their excuses, and demands hostages, and a few are given at once.
Four days later the cavalry ships set sail, but a sudden storm drives them back. That night the moon is full, and the high tide floods the ships on the beach and wrecks the others at anchor.

The Britons see that the Romans have few men, no horses and no grain, and they decide to wait for winter. But Caesar quietly gathers grain, repairs the ships with wood and metal from the wrecks, and loses only twelve ships.

The Britons ambush the seventh legion as it cuts grain, and Caesar, seeing the dust, hurries to rescue it. They fight from chariots, driving across the field, throwing spears and frightening the horses with the noise of the wheels.

The Britons are beaten again and promise to give twice as many hostages, and Caesar sails back to Gaul near the autumn equinox. When his report reaches Rome, the Senate orders twenty days of public thanksgiving.

In the winter Caesar orders his legions to build hundreds of ships, lower and wider than Roman ships usually are. The waves there are smaller, and wide ships can carry more horses and cargo, and they can be hauled ashore quickly.

Before he sails, Caesar marches to the land of the Treveri, who have not obeyed his orders and are talking with the Germans. Their chief Indutiomarus gives hostages out of fear, and Caesar favours his rival, who is loyal to Rome.

Caesar decides to take Dumnorix with him to Britain, because he does not trust him to stay in Gaul. But Dumnorix rides away with the cavalry, and when Caesar's horsemen catch him, he fights and is killed.

Five legions and two thousand cavalry gather at Portus Itius, while Labienus stays in Gaul with three legions to guard the ports. The fleet sails at sunset, the wind drops at midnight, and the soldiers row hard to reach the landing place by noon.

The Romans land without a fight, because the Britons, frightened by the sight of so many ships, have gone to the hills. Caesar leaves a guard with the ships and marches by night, and at a river he beats the Britons who attack him.

Next morning riders bring bad news: a storm in the night has damaged the fleet, and about forty ships are lost. Caesar hurries back, has the ships hauled up inside one great fort, and spends ten days and nights on the work.

While Caesar is away, the Britons gather and choose Cassivellaunus as their commander. His land lies north of the Thames, about eighty miles from the sea, and he has often been at war with the other tribes.

Cassivellaunus will not fight a great battle, because the heavy Roman soldiers are stronger in a fair fight. His chariots attack the column from the side, then retreat, and the Britons jump down to fight on foot.
Caesar marches to the Thames, which can be crossed only at one place. Sharp stakes line the far bank and lie hidden under the water, but the cavalry and legions cross together, and the Britons flee.

Cassivellaunus sends most of his army home, keeps four thousand chariots, and drives the people and cattle out of the Romans' path. The Trinovantes, whose king he once killed, ask Caesar to protect their young prince Mandubracius and promise to obey him.

Other British tribes, seeing the Trinovantes protected, also give hostages and tell Caesar where Cassivellaunus keeps his stronghold. It lies in forest and marsh, but the Romans attack from two sides, and the Britons run away through the back.
Cassivellaunus orders four kings of Kent to attack the Roman camp by the sea. The Romans rush out of the camp, kill many Britons, and capture one of their leaders.

Cassivellaunus asks for peace through Commius, and Caesar, who must return to Gaul before winter, agrees. He demands hostages and a yearly payment, and he forbids Cassivellaunus to harm the Trinovantes.

Caesar takes the hostages and many prisoners back to Gaul, and he leaves no soldiers in Britain. In a letter, the orator Marcus Cicero says that the island has no silver, and that its only prize will be slaves.

Caesar describes the Britons, though much of it comes from hearsay, not from his own eyes. He says that those inland grow no grain, live on milk and meat, and colour their skin blue with woad for battle.
That summer there is little rain, and the grain harvest in Gaul is poor. Caesar therefore spreads his legions over several camps instead of one, in the lands of different tribes.

About two weeks after the legions arrive, Ambiorix and Catuvolcus attack the wood-cutters and then the camp itself. The Romans drive them off, and Ambiorix, who has failed by force, decides to use a trick.

Ambiorix tells the Roman envoys that he is grateful to Caesar, but that his people forced him to attack. He warns that all Gaul will attack the camps on the same day, and he offers Sabinus safe passage.
In the council that night, Cotta argues that the Romans must not leave their camp on the word of an enemy. Sabinus replies that waiting is more dangerous, and the argument goes on far into the night.

At dawn the long Roman column marches out, heavy with baggage, and Ambiorix's men wait in a deep valley. When the Romans are strung out, the Gauls attack from both sides, and the Romans cannot form a line.

Sabinus sees Ambiorix at a distance and sends an interpreter to ask for mercy, and Ambiorix replies that Sabinus may come and talk. When Sabinus goes with his officers, the Gauls surround and kill them, and Cotta also dies fighting.

That night the last Romans in the camp kill themselves, and only a few escape through the forest to Labienus. Ambiorix rides on to the Atuatuci and the Nervii, and he urges them to attack Quintus Cicero's camp.
The Nervii and their allies attack the camp of Quintus Cicero, and when they fail, they offer to talk. Cicero, who is sick, answers that Romans never accept terms from an enemy who is still armed.

Cicero's soldiers work through the night and build a hundred and twenty towers from the wood that they have cut for the camp. Next day the Gauls attack in greater numbers and fill the ditch, but the Romans throw them back.

As the siege goes on, the Nervii, who have learned from Roman prisoners, build ramps, towers and shelters of their own. Because the Roman huts have straw roofs, they hurl red-hot clay balls and burning javelins onto them, and the wind spreads the flames.

Two centurions, Titus Pullo and Lucius Vorenus, are rivals, and each wants to prove that he is the braver. Pullo charges out among the Gauls and falls wounded, and Vorenus runs out to save him, and both get back alive.

Cicero must get word to Caesar, but every messenger is caught and killed in sight of the camp. At last Vertico, a Nervian friendly to Rome, persuades his slave to carry a letter through the enemy lines.

Caesar receives the letter in the evening and orders other legions to come to him at once. At dawn he marches with two legions, only about seven thousand men, and the Gauls leave Cicero's camp to meet him.

Caesar builds a very small camp so that the Gauls will think he is afraid, and he makes the gates narrow. He also sends a letter in Greek tied to a javelin, which sticks in a tower and goes unseen for two days.
The Gauls attack the small camp, but the Romans burst out of every gate and rout them. Caesar then marches to Cicero's camp, where almost every soldier is wounded, and he praises Cicero and his men.

Indutiomarus, the Treveran chief, gathers an army and rides up to Labienus's camp, insulting the Romans every day. Labienus pretends to be afraid, but one day his hidden horsemen charge out and kill Indutiomarus, and the other Gauls scatter.
Gaul is restless, so Caesar raises two new legions and asks his political partner Pompey to lend him a third. In 53 BC he quickly punishes the Nervii and other tribes that have been planning revolt.

Caesar builds a second bridge over the Rhine, close to the first, in only a short time. The Suebi have withdrawn into a huge forest, so after a short stay Caesar goes back to Gaul and leaves guards at the bridge.

Here Caesar interrupts the story to describe the Gauls, who, he says, honour only two classes of people. These are the Druids, who are priests and judges, and the knights, who fight, while the common people have almost no say.

The Druids judge disputes, lead the sacrifices, and teach young men, some of whom study for twenty years. They learn many verses by heart and never write them down, because they want knowledge to stay secret and memories to stay strong.

Caesar says that the Gauls worship many gods, and that the one they honour most is Mercury. He uses Roman names, such as Apollo, Mars, Jupiter and Minerva, for gods that the Gauls knew by their own names.
Caesar says that the Germans have no Druids and live mostly by hunting and war. No man owns fixed land, because their leaders share it out anew each year, so that no one grows rich or settles down.

The Hercynian Forest, Caesar says, is so wide that a man travelling light needs nine days to cross it. Its animals are strange: there is a one-horned deer, and an elk that, Caesar wrongly believes, has no joints in its legs.
Caesar returns to punish the Eburones, and he invites neighbouring tribes to plunder their land. Ambiorix escapes again and again, sometimes by luck, and he is never caught.

While Caesar is hunting the Eburones, German horsemen called the Sugambri cross the Rhine and suddenly attack the camp at Atuatuca. Many foragers are cut down before they can get back, but the camp is saved by the courage of the sick and the wounded.
