In early 52 BC, rioting in Rome follows the murder of the politician Clodius, and Caesar is held in northern Italy. The Gauls believe that he cannot return to his army, and the nobles plan a revolt in secret meetings in the forests.

On a fixed day the Carnutes attack the town of Cenabum and kill the Roman traders there, including an officer named Gaius Fufius Cita. The news is shouted from village to village, and it reaches the Arverni that same evening, over a hundred miles away.

Vercingetorix is a young noble of the Arverni, and his father Celtillus was killed for trying to become king. When his uncle and other nobles drive him out of the town, he gathers poor and desperate men, and they proclaim him king.
Vercingetorix demands hostages, soldiers and weapons from every state that joins him. He rules with great severity, and many peoples of western Gaul soon give him supreme command.
Caesar hears the news in Italy and wonders how he can reach his legions in the far north. He hurries to the Roman Province, which is in danger, and puts guards in its towns.
The Cevennes mountains are covered with snow six feet deep, and the Arverni think that they are safe. Caesar's soldiers dig a path through the snow, and he appears suddenly in the Arverni's land.
At a council, Vercingetorix says that Caesar cannot win without food. He urges the Gauls to burn their own farms and villages wherever the Romans might look for supplies.

The Bituriges burn more than twenty of their own towns in a single day, and other tribes do the same. They beg Vercingetorix to spare Avaricum, the most beautiful town in Gaul, and at last he agrees to defend it.
Caesar joins his army, takes a town called Vellaunodunum, and then storms Cenabum at night. His soldiers plunder and burn Cenabum to avenge the murder of the Roman traders, and the army marches on.

Caesar camps near Avaricum, but the Gauls have burned the grain, and the Boii send very little. For days the soldiers have no bread and live on meat, yet they never complain, even when Caesar offers to end the siege.

Avaricum is almost surrounded by a river and a marsh, and only one narrow way leads up to it. Its wall is built of beams and stones laid in layers, which fire cannot burn easily and rams cannot break.

While Vercingetorix stays in the countryside and attacks Roman foragers, Caesar's soldiers build a huge earth ramp against the wall. It takes twenty-five days, and it is about three hundred and thirty feet wide and eighty feet high.

The Gauls, who are skilled in mining, dig tunnels under the ramp and pull away its timber with iron hooks. They also throw burning pitch and tallow onto the Roman towers, and the fighting goes on day and night.

A Gaul on the wall hands burning balls of tallow and pitch to his friends until a Roman bolt strikes him down. A second man steps over him and takes his place, and then a third, so that the fire never stops.

Then heavy rain begins to fall, and the Gaulish guards on the wall relax, because they think that no one will attack in such weather. Caesar notices this and quietly tells his soldiers to prepare, promising rewards to the first men over the wall.
At a signal the Roman soldiers rush up the ramp and over the wall. The Gauls, taken by surprise, are driven from the wall, and they flee through the town and out of the gates.
The Romans, angry about Cenabum and the long siege, spare no one in Avaricum. Of about forty thousand people in the town, only eight hundred reach Vercingetorix's camp.
Vercingetorix is not discouraged, and he reminds the Gauls that he wanted Avaricum burned. The Gauls, who admire his calm, send more troops, and his fame grows.

Two Aedui both claim to be the chief magistrate, and Caesar goes to settle the quarrel and to ask for cavalry and grain. After that he divides his army: Labienus takes four legions north, and Caesar takes six toward Gergovia.

Vercingetorix breaks every bridge over the river Allier and marches along the opposite bank, matching every Roman step. Caesar hides some soldiers in a wood, they repair a broken bridge while the Gauls move on, and the army crosses.

Gergovia stands on a high mountain with steep slopes on every side, and Caesar sees that he cannot take it by storm. Instead he notices a hill near the town that is lightly guarded, captures it in a night attack, and builds a small camp there.

Ten thousand Aeduan soldiers march toward Caesar's camp, led by a noble named Litaviccus. Thirty miles from Gergovia, Litaviccus calls a halt and tells them a lie, that Caesar has put their leaders Eporedorix and Viridomarus to death.

Eporedorix and Viridomarus tell Caesar what Litaviccus has done, and Caesar sets out at once with four legions. He marches about twenty-five miles, finds the Aeduan column, shows the soldiers the two men alive, and the Aedui give in.

Caesar hurries back to Gergovia, where the Romans have been fighting hard all day and are nearly exhausted. Seeing that the Gauls have left one side of the mountain thinly defended, he plans a sudden attack on their camps.
The Roman soldiers take three Gaulish camps so quickly that King Teutomatus, who is asleep, escapes half dressed. But they ignore Caesar's order to stop and run up the slope to the town wall.
Gaulish women on the wall throw down clothes and silver and beg the Romans not to harm them. Some soldiers climb the wall, and for a moment the town seems to be theirs.

Marcus Petronius, a centurion, tries to break down a gate, but the Gauls are too many. Knowing that he cannot escape, he tells his men that he will save their lives, charges the Gauls, and dies as they get away.

Lucius Fabius, who was first on the wall at Avaricum, is lifted up by his friends again, but he is overwhelmed. More Gauls arrive, the Romans are driven down the slope, and forty-six centurions are lost.

The next day Caesar scolds the soldiers for ignoring the signal and for acting as if they could judge the battle better than their general. But he praises their courage, and says that he values discipline as much as bravery.
After Gergovia, the Aedui, long the friends of Rome, turn against Caesar and join Vercingetorix. At Noviodunum they kill the Roman traders, seize the hostages and Caesar's baggage, and burn the town.

Labienus leaves Agedincum with four legions and marches down the Seine toward Lutetia, the town of the Parisii on an island. Camulogenus, an old Gaulish leader, waits behind a marsh that no army can cross, and Labienus fails to build a road through it.
Labienus marches back up the river to Metiosedum, where he finds about fifty boats. He seizes them, loads soldiers into them, and takes the town without a fight.

Camulogenus hears of this, burns Lutetia and its bridges, and camps on the river bank opposite Labienus. News arrives that Caesar has been beaten at Gergovia and that the Aedui have rebelled, so Labienus is in danger of being cut off.

In the night Labienus sends five cohorts upstream, with the baggage animals, to make as much noise as they can. Meanwhile three legions slip quietly across the river lower down in the boats, and the Gauls do not notice.

The Gauls come to meet the Romans on the far bank, and in a fierce battle the seventh legion breaks their line. Camulogenus dies fighting among his men, and almost none of the Gauls who stand with him escape.

At a great council at Bibracte, the Gauls confirm Vercingetorix as leader of the whole war. He demands fifteen thousand horsemen to cut the Romans' supplies, and he sends the Aedui to attack the Allobroges.

Caesar has lost his Gallic cavalry, so he sends across the Rhine for German horsemen and light foot soldiers who can fight beside them. The German horses are poor, so Caesar gives them the horses of his officers and sets out for the Province.

Vercingetorix places his horsemen in three groups and attacks the Roman column, but Caesar also divides his cavalry in three. The German horsemen on the right take a ridge and drive the Gauls down, and then the whole Gaulish cavalry flees.

Vercingetorix gives up the battle and leads his army toward Alesia, the town of the Mandubii. Caesar follows, kills about three thousand of the Gaulish rearguard on the way, and camps near the town the next day.

Alesia stands on the top of a high hill, with a river on two sides and steep slopes all round. In front of it is a plain about three miles long, and hills as high as the town's hill surround the other sides.

Before the Romans can finish their walls, Vercingetorix sends his horsemen away by night to bring help from every tribe. He has only thirty days of grain, so he orders it to be shared out in small amounts.
Caesar sees that Alesia cannot be taken by storm, so he decides to starve it out. There are about eighty thousand picked men inside, and he starts to build a ring of siege works around the hill.

The inner line of the Roman works is eleven miles long, with twenty-three forts where soldiers stand guard by day. In front is a ditch twenty feet wide with straight sides, and behind it rises a rampart twelve feet high.

In front of the ditches the Romans plant sharpened tree trunks, which the soldiers call tombstones. They also dig pits, which they call lilies, with sharp stakes inside, and bury iron hooks that they call goads.

Caesar then builds a second line of the same kind, facing outward, fourteen miles long, to protect his army from a relief force. He also stores grain and fodder for thirty days, so that his men will not have to go out to forage.

The Gaulish leaders decide not to call out every fighting man, because a crowd so large could not be fed. According to Caesar, each tribe sends a fixed number, and the total is two hundred and fifty thousand foot soldiers and eight thousand horsemen.
Inside Alesia, the day on which help should arrive comes and goes, and the grain is almost finished. The Gauls hold a council to decide whether to surrender or to break out.

Critognatus, a noble of the Arverni, rises in the council and speaks fiercely against surrender. He reminds them that their fathers held out against the Cimbri and Teutones through the worst hunger, and he urges the same courage now.
The council rejects this idea, but it decides to send away everyone who cannot fight. The Mandubii, who own the town, are forced to leave with their wives and children.

The Mandubii come to the Roman wall in tears, and they beg to be taken as slaves if only they are fed. Caesar sets guards along the ramparts with orders to let no one in, so the people are left stranded between the lines.

The Gaulish relief army, led by Commius and three other chiefs, camps on a hill less than a mile from the Roman lines. The people in Alesia see their friends and cheer, and Vercingetorix leads his men out to the ditches.

Next day, the Gauls fill the plain with cavalry and archers, while the defenders in Alesia watch from the walls. The battle lasts until almost sunset, when the German horsemen charge and drive the archers off.

After a day spent making ladders and hooks, the Gauls approach at midnight and shout to warn the besieged. They hurl stones and arrows, but the Romans under Mark Antony and Trebonius throw them back, and the Gauls retreat before dawn.

The Gaulish chiefs send scouts to look for a weak spot, and they find a camp on a slope of a hill to the north. They pick sixty thousand of their best men and put Vercassivellaunus, a cousin of Vercingetorix, in command.

At noon the sixty thousand come down the hill, while the Gaulish cavalry rides onto the plain and the main army advances. Inside Alesia, Vercingetorix leads his men out, and the Romans must defend both lines at once.
The fighting goes on in every part of the lines, and the shouts of the Gauls behind the Romans frighten them. Caesar watches from a high place and sends help wherever the danger is greatest.

On the northern hill, the Gauls throw earth into the ditches and press hard, and the weary Romans run short of missiles. Caesar sends Brutus with cohorts, then Fabius with more, and at last he decides to go himself.
The soldiers on the hill recognise Caesar by his general's cloak, which he always wears in battle. When he arrives with fresh troops, the Romans cheer, and the shout is taken up along the whole line.

Labienus gathers eleven cohorts at the northern camp and prepares for a sortie, and Caesar hurries to join him. Caesar attacks, while the cavalry, sent round the outside of the works, charges the Gauls from behind.

The Gaulish army breaks, and the Roman cavalry chase the fugitives, killing many and capturing a great number. Vercingetorix, watching from the walls, leads his men back into Alesia, and the rest of the relief army scatters to its homes.

Vercingetorix tells the people of Alesia that he fought for the freedom of Gaul, not for himself. They may kill him or hand him over, he says, and they send envoys, and Caesar demands their weapons and their leaders.

Caesar sets aside the Aedui and Arverni prisoners, about twenty thousand men, to win back these two strong peoples. All the other prisoners are given to the soldiers, one to each man, and Rome orders twenty days of thanksgiving.

In 51 BC the Bellovaci and some other tribes rise once more, but Caesar wears them down, and their leader Correus is killed. These events are told in a final book written by Hirtius, an officer who served under Caesar.
The last stronghold is Uxellodunum, a hill town with a good spring at its foot. Caesar's engineers dig a tunnel under the spring and cut off the water, and the thirsty defenders surrender.

Hirtius says that in his last year in Gaul, Caesar chooses gentle ways, because he wants a peaceful province. He praises the states, gives gifts to their leaders and asks for no new burdens, and Gaul, worn out by war, stays quiet.

After Alesia, Vercingetorix is kept a prisoner in Rome for about six years. In 46 BC he is led through the city in Caesar's triumph, and the historian Cassius Dio says that he was put to death afterwards.

In 49 BC Caesar's enemies in the Senate demand that he give up his army, and he leads it across the Rubicon into Italy. Gallic cavalry and veterans of the Gallic war fight beside him in the civil war that follows.
Caesar wrote the Gallic War himself, and he calls himself Caesar, as if a calm observer were describing him. This makes the book sound fair, but it shows only his side of the story.

Caesar's numbers are often too big, but digging has shown that his description of Alesia is largely right. In the 1860s and again in the 1990s, diggers found Roman ditches, pits and weapons at Alise-Sainte-Reine in France.

After eight years of war, Gaul became part of the Roman world, and Roman roads soon crossed it. The people slowly learned Latin, and the Gaul of Vercingetorix became, over the centuries, the France that we know today.
C1C2: Caesar opens his account with a sentence that schoolchildren have copied for two thousand years: Gaul, taken as a whole, is divided into three parts. In one live the Belgae, in another the Aquitani, and in the third the people whom the Romans call Gauls and who call themselves Celts. Each has its own language, its own customs and its own laws, and the great rivers Garonne, Marne and Seine mark the borders between the three parts of the country.

Of all these peoples, Caesar declares, the Belgae are the bravest, and he is quick to explain why. They live farthest from the refinement of the Roman Province, so traders seldom reach them with the luxuries that soften a warrior's spirit. They are also close neighbours of the Germans across the Rhine, with whom they are perpetually at war.

Among the Helvetii, the people of what is now Switzerland, the richest and best-born man was Orgetorix. He told them that the mountains, the Rhine and the great lake hemmed them in on every side, and that a people so brave deserved wider lands. His words fell on willing ears, for the Helvetii were a proud, restless and warlike people.

The Helvetii spent two years gathering wagons, draught animals and grain, and then fixed the date of their departure. Meanwhile Orgetorix, who dreamed of ruling his own people, secretly bound the nobles Casticus and Dumnorix to a pact of mutual support. Each would seize power at home, and together, he thought, they would rule most of Gaul.

When the plot was betrayed, the Helvetii ordered Orgetorix to defend himself in chains, knowing that the penalty for such a crime was to be burned alive. He arrived at the trial with ten thousand followers and slipped out of danger, but he died soon afterwards, and the Helvetii suspected that he had taken his own life. His death did nothing to change their purpose, and the preparations went on exactly as before.

Determined to leave, the Helvetii burned their twelve towns, about four hundred villages and every store of grain that they could not carry. Caesar says that they did this so that, with no homes to return to, they would be readier to face any danger. Neighbouring peoples were persuaded to burn their own homes and to join the march.

After the war, the Romans found in the Helvetian camp a list written in Greek letters that named every man, woman and child who had left home. By this reckoning, three hundred and sixty-eight thousand people had set out, though modern historians suspect that the true figure was smaller. Caesar's numbers, in general, are far easier to quote than they are to believe, and the text will say so again.

Two roads lay open to the Helvetii when they began their long journey westward. One wound through the narrow pass of the Jura, and the Sequani, who lived there, were unlikely to allow so many strangers to pass; the other ran through the Roman Province beside the Rhône, and it was far shorter. The Helvetii chose the shorter one, and that choice led them straight toward the city of Geneva.

The news reached Caesar while he was still close to Rome, and it alarmed him at once. He saw that a whole people, armed and angry, marching through southern Gaul would threaten every Roman town in the region. There was no time to lose, and he did not intend to waste a single day.

Caesar left the city and travelled toward Further Gaul by the longest possible stages. When he arrived, he found only a single legion in the whole province, a force far too small to stop three hundred thousand people. He therefore ordered the province to raise as many soldiers as it could, and he rode on to Geneva.

On reaching Geneva, Caesar at once ordered the bridge across the Rhône to be broken down. When Helvetian envoys came to ask for a peaceful passage through the Province, he replied that he needed time to consider and told them to return after two weeks. The delay was no courtesy, since Caesar needed every day he could gain to gather soldiers and prepare his defence.

Along the Roman bank of the Rhône, Caesar's soldiers raised a wall sixteen feet high, with a deep ditch dug in front of it. It ran for nearly nineteen miles, from Lake Geneva to the Jura mountains, and forts were built at short intervals along its length. Caesar posted his men in them, so that any attempt to cross could be met at once by troops who were already in position.

When the Helvetii returned, Caesar told them bluntly that Roman custom did not allow any army to march through the Province, and that he would stop them by force if they tried. They did try, by day and by night, with boats lashed together and at the shallow fords, but the Roman wall and the missiles from the forts defeated every attempt. In the end they gave up the idea of crossing the Rhône at all.

The Helvetii now turned to the second road, which led through the narrow pass between the Jura mountains and the Rhône, and for this they needed the Sequani's consent. Dumnorix, who was well liked among the Sequani and had married the daughter of Orgetorix, won it for them. The two peoples exchanged hostages, the Sequani promising not to block the pass and the Helvetii promising to do no harm on the way.

Caesar was told that the Helvetii meant to march west toward the Santones, whose country lay close to the borders of the Province, and this was a danger he could not accept. He left Labienus in command of the wall, hurried to northern Italy, raised two new legions and called out three more from winter quarters near Aquileia. With these five legions he crossed the Alps by the shortest road, beating back the mountain tribes that tried to block him.

Meanwhile the Helvetii had marched through the country of the Sequani and begun to plunder the fields of the Aedui, who were old friends and allies of the Roman people. Unable to defend their farms, the Aedui sent messengers to Caesar to beg for protection. Their plea was the sort of appeal that Caesar liked best, since it gave his campaign the look of a duty rather than an invasion.

Learning that three quarters of the Helvetii had already crossed the Saône, Caesar led three legions out at night against the rest, who were still waiting on the near bank, burdened with baggage and unprepared. Most of them were cut down where they stood, and the few survivors fled into the woods. They belonged to the Tigurini, the clan that had killed a Roman consul in 107 BC and forced his army to pass beneath the yoke, so Caesar was glad to settle an old account.

Caesar's soldiers then built a bridge across the Saône in a single day, a task that had cost the Helvetii twenty days of hard labour with their rafts. The Helvetii were struck with amazement at the speed with which the Romans had done what they themselves had found almost impossible. Alarmed, they sent envoys to Caesar, led by Divico, who had commanded their army against Cassius long ago.

Divico, speaking for his people, said that if the Romans would make peace, the Helvetii would go and settle wherever Caesar chose. If Caesar preferred war, however, he should remember the disaster that the Romans had once suffered at Helvetian hands, and the courage that had won it. He added that Caesar must not be too proud of destroying one clan by surprise, for the Helvetii had been taught by their fathers to rely on valour rather than on tricks.

Caesar answered that he remembered the old defeat all too well, and that it was the worse for Rome because it had been undeserved. If the Helvetii would give hostages and make amends to the Aedui and their allies for the damage done, he would agree to peace. Divico replied that the Helvetii had been taught by their ancestors to take hostages, not to give them, and with that the talks were over.

Caesar sent his cavalry, about four thousand horsemen raised from the Gallic allies, to find out which way the Helvetii were heading. They rode too far in pursuit of the enemy's rear and ran into only five hundred Helvetian riders, who drove them back with a few losses. Proud of having beaten so many with so few, the Helvetii began to turn and challenge the Romans more and more boldly.

For about fifteen days Caesar followed the Helvetii, keeping his army five or six miles behind them and refusing to fight on unfavourable ground. Meanwhile the grain that the Aedui had promised failed to arrive, for the Aedui were always about to send it and never did. With the army marching farther from its sources of supply each day, the shortage was becoming dangerous.

At last Caesar summoned Liscus, the chief magistrate of the Aedui, and demanded to know why the grain had not come. Liscus, afraid of speaking, admitted at length that the real cause was Dumnorix, a man who was rich, popular and passionately hostile to Rome. Dumnorix, he said, commanded the Aeduan cavalry, had grown wealthy on the tolls of the country, and was ruining Caesar's supplies in the hope of becoming a king.

Caesar then sent for Diviciacus, the brother of Dumnorix, who was a faithful friend of Rome and a man he trusted. Diviciacus embraced him in tears and begged him not to punish his brother, admitting that everything Liscus had said was true. Caesar, unwilling to hurt so loyal an ally, forgave Dumnorix, but he warned him plainly and set guards to watch his every move.

Hearing that the Helvetii had camped eight miles away, Caesar sent Labienus with two legions to climb the hill above them in the dark, and he followed with the rest. All would have gone well had not Considius, a scout who had a name for experience, galloped back at dawn and sworn that the hill was held by Gauls. Caesar, trusting the report, drew his army off to safer ground, and later discovered that the hill had been in Roman hands all the while.

With only two days of grain left, Caesar gave up the chase and turned toward Bibracte, the largest and richest town of the Aedui, about eighteen miles away. A deserter from the Gallic cavalry carried word of this to the Helvetii, who were quick to put their own meaning on the manoeuvre. Thinking that the Romans were running away for fear of battle, the Helvetii turned about and began to harass the Roman rear.

Seeing the enemy approach, Caesar drew his army up on a hill and ordered his own horse to be led out of sight, and then the horses of all his officers. By making the danger equal for every man, he took away any hope of flight. He placed his four veteran legions in three lines halfway up the slope and the two new ones, with the allied troops, at the top.

The Helvetii advanced in a close mass, shields locked together, and the Roman javelins fell on them from above. Many of the heavy javelins pierced two shields at once and pinned them together, and as the iron points bent, the Gauls could not pull them free. Some threw their shields away and fought uncovered, until the Romans drew their swords and drove them back to a hill about a mile off.

As the Romans pressed forward, about fifteen thousand men of the Boii and the Tulingi, who had been guarding the Helvetian rear, came up and fell on the Roman right flank. Seeing this, the beaten Helvetii turned back and fought again, so that the Romans had to form two fronts, the third line facing the new threat. The fight lasted from the early afternoon until night, and for all that time not one Helvetian was seen to turn his back.

The battle swept on to the great circle of wagons that the Helvetii had made their fort, and there the fighting was fiercest of all. From the wagons and from between the wheels, men threw spears and women and children hurled stones, and they died there where they stood. Late in the night the Romans took the camp, and about a hundred and thirty thousand Helvetii slipped away into the darkness.

Caesar rested for three days to bury the dead and tend the wounded, and he warned the Lingones not to help the Helvetii. With no food and nowhere to go, the Helvetii surrendered, handing over their hostages, their weapons and the slaves who had run away to them. Caesar sent them home to rebuild their burnt towns, and the census showed that only about a hundred and ten thousand of the three hundred and sixty-eight thousand were left.

Chiefs from nearly every state in Gaul came to congratulate Caesar, saying that although he had punished the Helvetii for old wrongs to Rome, his victory had been as useful to Gaul as to the Roman people. They then asked for leave to hold a secret meeting, and when Caesar agreed, they threw themselves at his feet. Diviciacus, the Aeduan, spoke for them all, weeping, and told the story of a king whom they feared far more than the Helvetii.

Diviciacus explained that the Sequani, to win a war against the Aedui, had invited fifteen thousand Germans across the Rhine, and that these guests had liked the rich land so well that they had stayed. By now, he said, there were about a hundred and twenty thousand of them in Gaul, and their king, Ariovistus, had seized a third of the Sequani's land and was demanding another third. The Aedui had lost their hostages, their best families and almost all of their power.

Only the Sequani said nothing and stood with their eyes fixed on the ground, and Caesar was puzzled until Diviciacus explained that they were too frightened even to complain. Ariovistus, he said, was cruel to all who displeased him, and the Sequani's towns lay under his guard. Caesar resolved to act, for Rome could not let her friends the Aedui be ruined, and he sent envoys to ask the German king to meet him.

Ariovistus answered that if Caesar wanted anything he should come to him, and that he had no mind to visit the Romans. When Caesar demanded that no more Germans cross the Rhine and that the Aedui be left in peace, the king replied that the right of war allowed conquerors to rule as they pleased, exactly as Rome did. If Caesar attacked, he added, the Romans would learn what Germans who had not slept under a roof for fourteen years could do.

More bad news followed, for fresh German tribes called the Harudes were ravaging the Aedui, and the Suebi were gathering on the bank of the Rhine. Fearing that Ariovistus would reach the supplies of the Sequani first, Caesar marched by day and night to Vesontio, the largest town in their country. It was strong by nature, since a loop of the river Doubs almost surrounded it, and a high hill closed the gap.

While the army rested at Vesontio, Gauls and traders kept telling the soldiers about the Germans, men of enormous size, with terrible courage and eyes that no one could face in battle. Fear began among the young officers, who had joined the army only for the sake of friendship with Caesar, and it spread from tent to tent. Some made excuses to go home, some stayed but wept, and many sat in their quarters writing their wills.

Caesar called together the centurions of every rank and scolded them sharply for presuming to ask where they were going or why. Ariovistus, he reminded them, had sought the friendship of Rome in the past, and the Germans had been beaten before by Marius, and even the Helvetii had often defeated them. If no one else would follow, he would march with the tenth legion alone, for he knew that its loyalty would never fail him.

The tenth legion was the first to answer, thanking Caesar warmly for his trust and promising to be ready for battle. The other legions, ashamed of their fears, then sent their officers to explain that they had never doubted his judgement or his courage. Reassured, Caesar set out with the whole army and marched for seven days, until his scouts reported that the Germans were not more than twenty-four miles away.

Ariovistus, hearing how close the Romans were, now asked for the meeting that he had refused before, and Caesar agreed to it. Since he did not dare to trust his own safety to the Gallic cavalry, Caesar took their horses and gave them to soldiers of the tenth legion. One of these men joked that Caesar was doing more than he had promised, for he had promised them a place as his guard and was now making them knights.

On a large mound in an open plain, Caesar and Ariovistus met on horseback, each with only ten horsemen to guard him. Caesar reminded the king that the Roman Senate had named him a friend of Rome, and demanded that he bring no more Germans over the Rhine. Ariovistus answered that he had come only by invitation and would conquer as he pleased, and when his horsemen began to hurl stones and spears at the Romans, Caesar ended the meeting at once.

Ariovistus soon asked for a second meeting, but Caesar, not wishing to risk another conference, refused to go himself. He sent instead Gaius Valerius Procillus, a Gaul who held the rights of a Roman citizen, and Marcus Mettius, a friend of the king's. Ariovistus accused them of being spies and threw them into chains before they had finished speaking.

Prisoners revealed to Caesar why Ariovistus kept avoiding battle: the women of his people, by casting lots and watching the eddies of the rivers, had declared that heaven would forbid a victory before the new moon. Caesar saw at once that this was the moment to strike, and he led his men up to the German camp in battle order. The Germans, forced to leave their defences, drew themselves up tribe by tribe, with their wagons behind them so that no man could think of running away.

The Romans ran forward so fast that the Germans had no time to hurl their spears, and the two armies were at once fighting hand to hand with swords. The Germans formed a close line and locked their shields above their heads, but Roman soldiers leaped up on top of them, tore the shields down and stabbed the men beneath. On the Roman right the enemy gave way and fled, though on the left the Germans, who were more numerous there, began to drive the Romans back.

Young Publius Crassus, who commanded the cavalry, was not caught up in the fighting and could see how badly the Roman left was pressed. Without waiting for orders from Caesar, he sent the third line of soldiers to help, and this fresh force restored the battle. The Germans who had been winning there turned and ran, and the whole of their army broke.

The Germans fled toward the Rhine, about five miles away, and the Roman cavalry rode down many of them on the way. Ariovistus found a small boat tied to the bank and escaped in it, but two of his wives and one of his daughters died in the flight, and another daughter was captured. Of the great German army, very few ever reached the safety of the far bank of the Rhine.

As the Roman cavalry hunted the fugitives, Caesar came upon Procillus, who was being dragged along in triple chains by his guards. He said afterwards that the sight gave him as much pleasure as the victory itself, since a man he valued and trusted had been rescued from the worst. Procillus told him that the lots had been cast three times to decide whether he should be burned alive, and that each time the lots had saved him.

When the news of the victory spread, the Suebi who had gathered on the near bank of the Rhine began to go home, and the Ubii, who lived beside them, attacked them as they went. Caesar had ended two wars in a single summer, and he now put his army into winter quarters in the land of the Sequani. Leaving Labienus in command, he went to northern Italy to hold the law courts, as a governor was expected to do.

All through the winter, rumours reached Caesar in northern Italy, and Labienus confirmed them in his letters: the Belgae were swearing oaths and exchanging hostages. They feared that once the Romans had pacified the rest of Gaul, they would turn on the north, and some Gauls who disliked Roman rule encouraged them. Caesar raised two new legions, sent them north at the beginning of summer, and followed to take command himself.

The Remi, who lived nearest to Caesar, gave him hostages and promised him supplies, and they warned him that the rest of the Belgae had raised an enormous army. Soon afterwards the Belgae surrounded the Remi town of Bibrax, only eight miles from the Roman camp, and tried to climb its wall under a roof of shields. Caesar sent Numidian and Cretan archers and Balearic slingers, and the Belgae, giving up hope, burned the villages round about and marched against the Roman camp.

Caesar pitched his camp on a ridge beside the river Aisne, with a marsh on one side, and he built a bridge and strong forts to protect his supplies. The Belgae, who had camped less than two miles away, tried to wade across a ford in the river to cut his line of communication. Roman cavalry and light troops met them in the water, killed many and drove the rest back, and the Belgae found themselves unable either to cross or to feed their huge army.

Hungry and quarrelsome, the Belgae decided to go home and to meet again in the country of whichever tribe the Romans attacked first. They left in the night, in great noise and confusion, each man pushing forward to be first, so that the army looked more like a rout than a march. Caesar, suspecting a trap, waited until daylight, and then he sent his cavalry after them and cut down the rearguard.

Caesar marched swiftly into the land of the Suessiones and attacked their town, Noviodunum, with ramps, shelters and a tall siege tower. The Gauls, who had never seen such machines, were amazed at how fast the Romans could build such works, and they surrendered at once. Soon the Bellovaci and the Ambiani also came to terms, Diviciacus having begged Caesar to be gentle with the Bellovaci.

The fiercest of all the Belgae were the Nervii, a people who would not allow traders to bring wine or luxuries into their country, since they believed that such things softened the spirit. They had no cavalry to speak of, and so they had long ago learned to plant hedges across their country, bending young trees and twining the branches to form a barrier that no horseman could cross. Together with their neighbours the Atrebates and the Viromandui, they planned to ambush the Romans as they marched.

The Roman army reached the river Sabis and began to build its camp on a hill that sloped down to the water, while the baggage was still arriving. On the far bank, thick woods hid the Nervii and their allies, who waited until the Roman soldiers had laid down their packs. Then they burst out of the trees, crossed the river in a few moments and were upon the Romans so quickly that they seemed to be in all places at once.

Caesar had to do everything at the same moment: raise the flag that was the signal for battle, sound the trumpet, recall the men who were out gathering wood and bring the rest into line. There was no time to put on helmets, to fit the crests, or even to take the leather covers from the shields. Each man took his place wherever he happened to be standing, under whichever standard he first saw.

Seizing a shield from a soldier in the rear ranks, for he had come without one of his own, Caesar pushed to the front, where the danger was greatest. He called the centurions by name and shouted encouragement to the men, ordering them to spread out so that they could use their swords. His presence, and the sight of their general fighting as a common soldier, gave new heart to the weary and wavering troops.

On the left, the ninth and tenth legions drove the Atrebates down the slope and into the river, and the eleventh and eighth did the same to the Viromandui in the centre. But on the right the Roman legions had been left with an open flank, and the whole body of the Nervii, led by their chiefs, poured through the gap and swarmed up toward the camp. The Gallic cavalry and the camp servants, seeing the Romans surrounded, fled in terror, and some carried the news far and wide that the Roman army was lost.

The Nervii in the front rank fell in heaps, but those behind climbed over the bodies of their comrades, and from that dreadful mound they hurled their spears and threw back the missiles that came at them. Labienus, who had captured the enemy camp across the river, saw from the high ground that the Roman camp was surrounded and sent the tenth legion running back to help. When the cavalry and the camp servants saw the legion approaching, they too found new courage, and the Nervii, though they fought desperately, were at last cut down.

The people of the Nervii were almost wiped out, if Caesar's figures are to be believed, for of their six hundred senators only three survived, and of sixty thousand fighting men only about five hundred. When the old men, the women and the children, who had been hidden in the marshes, sent envoys to beg for mercy, Caesar treated them kindly. He ordered the neighbouring peoples not to harm them and allowed them to keep their land and their towns.

The Atuatuci, who were descended from the Cimbri and Teutones, shut themselves up in a strongly fortified town on a high rock. When the Romans began to build a tall siege tower, they laughed from the walls, asking how such small men could hope to move so huge a machine. But when the tower began to roll toward them, they were so terrified that they sent envoys to beg for peace.

The Atuatuci threw so many weapons from the wall that the pile reached almost to the top of it, but they had hidden about a third of their arms. That night they burst out in a desperate attack on the Roman lines, and about four thousand of them were killed and the rest driven back. Their promise had been broken, and Caesar sold the whole population of the town, about fifty-three thousand people, as slaves.

Meanwhile Publius Crassus, with a single legion, had brought the tribes along the Atlantic coast under Roman rule, and most of the north of Gaul seemed to be at peace. When Caesar's report reached Rome, the Senate ordered fifteen days of public thanksgiving, an honour that no general had ever received before. Caesar went to northern Italy for the winter, believing that the war in Gaul was over.

Servius Galba, with the twelfth legion, had been sent to open the Alpine passes to merchants and wintered in the mountain town of Octodurus. One morning the camp woke to find that the Gauls had left in the night and had occupied the hills on every side, apparently intending to destroy a legion that was smaller than it should have been. After a long day's defence, Galba's men burst out of every gate at once, and the Gauls, taken by surprise, fled.

That winter, Crassus sent officers to the tribes of the coast to collect grain, and the Veneti, who were the greatest naval power of the region, seized two of them. They hoped to exchange these officers for the hostages they had given to the Romans, and other tribes soon followed their lead. Since the safety of envoys was sacred in the eyes of every nation, Caesar was determined to punish the Veneti, and he ordered warships to be built on the river Loire.

The Veneti lived in towns on tongues of land that the sea cut off at high tide and left stranded at low water, so that neither an army on foot nor a fleet of ships could easily reach them. Caesar's soldiers built great earth banks and walls against one town after another, but when the defenders despaired, they simply loaded their goods onto ships and sailed to the next town. This went on for much of the summer, and Caesar saw that only a victory at sea would end it.

The ships of the Veneti were built of oak, with beams a foot thick fastened by iron nails as thick as a thumb, and their anchors were held by iron chains instead of ropes. They used soft leather for sails, since, in Caesar's view, they had no canvas or did not know how to work it, and their high, broad hulls stood up well to storms. The Roman ships, which were lower, could not damage them by ramming, and Roman missiles struggled to reach so high a deck.

Decimus Brutus, who commanded the Roman fleet, had his sailors fasten sharp hooks, like those used to pull down walls, to the ends of long poles. With these they caught the ropes that held the yards of the enemy ships to their masts and rowed away as hard as they could, so that the ropes snapped. The great yards crashed down, and a Veneti ship that could not use her sails was helpless.

Then the wind failed altogether, and the great Veneti ships lay motionless on a flat sea, unable to flee. Two or three Roman ships closed around each of them, and the soldiers climbed aboard and fought hand to hand across the decks. From about ten in the morning until sunset the battle went on, and by evening almost the whole Veneti fleet, with all the young men of the tribe aboard, had been taken.

After this defeat the whole Veneti people surrendered, and Caesar, thinking that the lesson must be remembered, punished them with great severity. He had the senate of the Veneti put to death and sold the rest of the people into slavery, so that every tribe in Gaul would learn that the persons of envoys were sacred. In the same summer, Sabinus tricked the Unelli, and Crassus won a victory in Aquitania, so that the year closed with the north-west and south-west of Gaul under Roman control.

The Usipetes and Tencteri, two German peoples driven from their lands by the powerful Suebi after years of wandering, crossed the Rhine near the sea and entered Gaul. The Suebi, according to Caesar, were the largest and fiercest of the German tribes, with a hundred districts, each of which sent a thousand armed men to war every year. Caesar, knowing that the Gauls were quick to change sides and that some were already inviting the newcomers in, set out earlier than usual to join his army.

Caesar told the Germans that they might settle in the land of the Ubii, but he would not allow them to stay in Gaul, and they asked for a truce of three days to consider. During the truce, eight hundred German horsemen suddenly attacked five thousand Roman and Gallic cavalry and threw them into confusion. The Germans leaped from their horses to stab the Roman horses from underneath, and seventy-four Roman riders were killed.

Early the next morning, the German leaders and elders came in large numbers to Caesar's camp, apparently to apologise for the attack and to ask for a longer truce. Caesar, who considered that they had broken faith by attacking during a truce, ordered them to be arrested and marched out with all his legions, placing the cavalry at the rear. The Germans, with their leaders gone and no idea what to expect, were thrown into confusion.

The Germans were thrown into panic, for they could not form their line, and some took up their weapons while others tried to flee. Women and children ran out of the camp in every direction, and the Roman cavalry chased them down toward the place where the Meuse joins the Rhine, where many drowned. By Caesar's account, the German force numbered four hundred and thirty thousand, and not a single Roman was killed, a boast that modern historians treat with caution.

When the news reached Rome, the senator Cato, one of Caesar's fiercest critics, declared that Caesar had broken a truce and proposed that he be handed over to the Germans to clear the Roman people of the guilt. Caesar, who had other plans in mind and little patience for his critics, decided to cross the Rhine into Germany. The Ubii had begged him for help against the Suebi, and he wished to show the Germans that Roman armies could cross the great river and that they should fear what they found on the other side.

The Rhine was wide, deep and swift, and Caesar felt that to cross it in boats would be both unsafe and unworthy of the dignity of Rome. He therefore ordered his engineers to build a bridge, using a method that he describes in careful detail. Pairs of beams a foot and a half thick, sharpened at one end, were lowered into the river by machines and rammed into the bed at a slant, leaning downstream with the current.

Long timbers were laid across the beams, and over them rods and bundles of branches, so that within ten days of the first timber being brought to the bank the whole bridge was complete. To protect it against tree trunks and boats that the Germans might send floating down against it, the engineers drove a line of extra piles upstream, like a breakwater. Strong guards were posted at both ends, and the army, which had marched to the bank in perfect order, prepared to cross.

Caesar marched his army across the bridge into Germany, and the Sugambri, whose land lay nearest and who had sheltered the Germans who fled, left their homes and hid in the forests. Caesar burned their villages and farms and cut down the grain, and the Ubii, who wanted the Romans as protectors, gave him information about the Suebi. They had gathered all their fighting men at the centre of their country, he heard, and were waiting for the Romans to come.

After eighteen days in Germany, Caesar felt that he had achieved his purpose of frightening the Germans, and that it would be unwise to go further. The Suebi had withdrawn deep into their forests and refused to come out and fight, and the season was growing late. He led his army back across the bridge and cut it down behind him, so that no German could follow.

Summer was nearly over, but Caesar decided to sail to Britain, because in almost all his Gallic wars the Britons had sent help to his enemies. He questioned traders, but none of them knew the size of the island, the people who lived there or any harbour that could hold large ships. He therefore sent Gaius Volusenus, an officer he trusted, in a single warship to look at the coast, and Volusenus returned after five days with what he had learned.

Caesar sailed after midnight with the seventh and tenth legions on eighty transports, while eighteen more ships, waiting for the cavalry at another port, were held back by the wind. By about ten in the morning his fleet came in sight of Britain, where tall white cliffs rose from the sea. Armed Britons stood on every height, and the coast was so steep that spears could be thrown straight down on any ship that tried to land.

Caesar waited at anchor until about three in the afternoon for the rest of his ships to come up, and meanwhile he called his officers together. He warned them that everything must be done at a signal, since the sea would not wait for them. When wind and tide were both in his favour, he sailed about seven miles along the coast to an open, level beach, with the Britons following along the cliffs.

The large Roman ships could not come close to the shore, and the soldiers, weighed down with their heavy weapons, would have to leap into deep water, struggle to keep their footing and fight the enemy at the same time. The Britons, who knew the ground, stood on the dry beach or waded in a little way and hurled their spears with perfect freedom, while their horses were trained to splash through the shallows. The Roman soldiers, who had never faced such a landing, hesitated, and they did not show the eagerness that they usually showed in land battles.

Then the standard-bearer of the tenth legion, after praying to the gods for a happy outcome, cried out to his comrades to jump down, unless they wished to hand the eagle over to the enemy. He added that he, at least, would do his duty to the republic and to his general, and he leaped from the ship and carried the eagle toward the Britons. Seeing this, the soldiers, urging one another not to suffer such a disgrace, jumped down in great numbers.

On the beach the fighting was confused, because the soldiers, jumping down from different ships, could not find their own standards or join the right groups. The Britons, who knew the shallows, rode in to attack any lone soldier, so Caesar sent the warships' boats, filled with fresh men, wherever help was needed. Once the Romans had found firm ground and could stand together, they drove the Britons back, though without cavalry they could not chase them far.

Soon after the landing, British envoys came to Caesar to ask for peace, bringing with them Commius, the Atrebatian whom Caesar had sent ahead and whom the Britons had thrown into chains as soon as he stepped ashore. They put the blame on the common people and begged to be forgiven for what they had done. Caesar scolded them for having begun a war without cause, but he accepted their excuses and demanded hostages, some of whom were handed over at once.

Four days after the landing, the eighteen cavalry ships left Gaul in a gentle wind, but as they approached Britain a storm swept them back, and some were driven far down the coast. The same night there was a full moon, which always brings the highest tides of the Ocean, a fact that the Romans did not know. The sea flooded the warships that had been hauled up on the beach and battered the transports at anchor, and many were wrecked.

The British chiefs, seeing how few the Romans were, how small their camp was and how many of their ships lay wrecked, quietly left the camp and began to raise forces again. Caesar guessed what they intended, and he collected grain from the fields and had the damaged ships mended with wood and bronze from the ones that were beyond repair. By great labour his men saved all but twelve of the ships, and the rest were made fit for the voyage back.

While the seventh legion was cutting grain in a field, the Britons, who had hidden in the woods, fell upon the soldiers and surrounded them with horsemen and chariots. Seeing a great cloud of dust in the direction the legion had taken, Caesar guessed what had happened and hurried to the rescue with a few cohorts. The British charioteers first drove all over the field, hurling spears and frightening the horses with the noise of the wheels, and then the warriors leaped down to fight on foot while the drivers waited close by.

After one more battle, in which the Britons were beaten again, Caesar demanded twice as many hostages and sailed back near the autumn equinox, for his ships were leaky and the weather was turning. Two of his transports, carried farther down the coast, landed their soldiers among the Morini, who surrounded them until Caesar sent cavalry to the rescue. When his report reached Rome, the Senate ordered twenty days of public thanksgiving, though the Romans had seen only a strip of the coast and had not kept a foot of it.

Before leaving Gaul for Italy that winter, Caesar ordered his legions to build a great fleet, and he explained exactly how it was to be done. The ships were to be lower than those used in the Mediterranean, because the waves in the Channel were smaller, and wider, so that they could carry more horses and cargo and be hauled quickly up a beach. All were fitted with oars as well as sails, and the soldiers worked hard through the winter to finish them.

Before he sailed, Caesar marched with four legions and eight hundred cavalry into the country of the Treveri, who had ignored his summons and were said to be stirring up the Germans across the Rhine. Their two leaders were rivals, and while one of them came at once to explain himself, the other, Indutiomarus, held back until he saw that the Roman army was serious. Then he too came in and gave hostages, and Caesar, after taking them from all the leading families, left the loyal rival in charge.

Caesar decided to take Dumnorix with him to Britain, since he did not trust such a man to be left behind in Gaul. Dumnorix pleaded to stay, pretending to fear the sea and his religion, and when Caesar refused, he began to stir up the other nobles. At last he rode away with the Aeduan cavalry, and when Caesar's horsemen overtook him, he cried that he was a free man of a free state, and he was killed as he fought.

Five legions and two thousand cavalry gathered at Portus Itius, and Labienus was left behind in Gaul with three legions and another two thousand horsemen to guard the harbours, secure the grain and watch the tribes. Caesar set sail at sunset in a light south-west wind, but at midnight the wind dropped, and the tide carried the ships off course. At dawn he saw Britain on his left, far behind, and the soldiers rowed so hard that the heavy transports kept pace with the warships.

The Romans landed without opposition, for the Britons, terrified by the sight of so many ships, had withdrawn to the high ground. Caesar left ten cohorts and three hundred horsemen to guard the ships and marched through the night, and after about twelve miles he found the enemy at a river. The Britons, charging down from higher ground, were driven back by the Roman cavalry, and they retreated to a stronghold in the woods that the seventh legion captured with a ramp and a roof of shields.

The next morning messengers arrived with bad news: a storm in the night had dashed the ships against each other and the shore, and about forty were lost. Caesar hurried back to the coast, ordered all the ships to be hauled up and enclosed by one great fortification with the camp, and the soldiers worked day and night for about ten days. He also sent word to Labienus to build as many new ships as he could, and then he returned to his army.

During Caesar's absence, large British forces had gathered, and the tribes, forgetting their quarrels, agreed to give the supreme command to Cassivellaunus. His kingdom lay north of the river Thames, about eighty miles from the sea, and he had spent years in wars with the neighbouring peoples. The Britons, alarmed by the Roman landing, now saw that they must stand together.

Cassivellaunus knew that he could not beat the heavily armed Romans in a fair battle, and so he sent his chariots and horsemen to harass them on the march. The Romans, loaded with armour and tied to their ranks, found it hard to pursue an enemy who struck suddenly, retreated at speed and struck again from another side. When three legions and all the cavalry went out to forage, the Britons attacked in force, but the Romans beat them so thoroughly that they never again fought a large battle.

Caesar marched to the Thames, which could be crossed on foot at only one place, and even there with difficulty. On the far bank Cassivellaunus had drawn up a great force, and the bank itself was lined with sharp stakes, while others were hidden under the water. The Romans sent the cavalry across first and the legions after them, advancing with only their heads above the water, and the Britons, unable to resist such a charge, fled.

Cassivellaunus, giving up the hope of a pitched battle, dismissed most of his army and kept about four thousand chariots, with which he watched the Romans' march and drove the people and cattle from their path. Meanwhile the Trinovantes, one of the strongest peoples of that region, sent envoys to Caesar. Their king had been killed by Cassivellaunus, and his son Mandubracius had fled to Caesar for protection, so they now offered obedience in return for that young man's safety.

Seeing that the Trinovantes had been protected, five more British peoples sent envoys to surrender, and they told Caesar where to find the stronghold of Cassivellaunus, hidden in forest and protected by marsh. It was crowded with people and cattle, and the Romans attacked it from two sides at once. The Britons, after a short resistance, rushed out of the other side of the fort and left behind many of their cattle, which fell into Roman hands.

Cassivellaunus, who had little left to hope for, sent messengers to the four kings of Kent, whose names were Cingetorix, Carvilius, Taximagulus and Segovax, and told them to gather their forces and attack the Roman naval camp. The Britons advanced against the camp, but the Romans sallied out, killed many of them and took prisoner a noble leader named Lugotorix. The attack had failed completely, and the king's last hope had failed with it.

Cassivellaunus, worn down by these defeats and by the desertion of his allies, sent envoys to Caesar through Commius to ask for peace. Caesar, who knew that the sailing season was short and that Gaul was restless, agreed to talk. He demanded hostages and a yearly payment to the Roman people, and he forbade the king to harm Mandubracius or the Trinovantes.

Caesar took hostages from the British peoples and, since many of his ships had been lost or damaged, carried his army back to Gaul in two crossings. By a piece of good fortune, not a single ship that carried soldiers was lost in either voyage, though several of the empty ones that returned for the second load failed to arrive. Cicero, the famous Roman orator, whose brother Quintus served with Caesar, wrote to a friend that the island held no silver and that the only booty to be expected there was slaves.

Caesar pauses to describe the Britons, though much of what he says came to him second-hand, and he notes that the people of Kent, who lived nearest the sea, were much like the Gauls. Those of the interior sowed no grain and lived on milk and meat, and they dyed their bodies blue with woad, which made them look terrible in battle. They wore their hair long and shaved everything except the head and upper lip, and, Caesar adds, groups of ten or twelve men shared wives, a claim that careful readers doubt.

That summer there had been little rain, and the harvest in Gaul was poor, so Caesar could not feed his whole army in one place. He therefore placed his legions in several winter camps in different parts of the country, each only a few days' march from the next. Sabinus and Cotta, with a legion and five more cohorts, went to Atuatuca, in the country of the Eburones, which was ruled by two chiefs, Ambiorix and Catuvolcus.

About a fortnight after the Romans had arrived, Ambiorix and Catuvolcus, who had until then seemed friendly, suddenly attacked the soldiers who were cutting wood and then came on to attack the camp itself. The Romans quickly took up arms, drove the Gauls off and killed a good many of them with the help of the cavalry. Ambiorix, who had failed by force, now decided to try a trick, and he asked to speak to a Roman officer.

Ambiorix told the Roman envoys that he owed a great deal to Caesar, who had rescued his son and his nephew from the Atuatuci, and that the attack on the camp had been his people's decision, not his own. All of Gaul, he said, had agreed to attack the Roman winter camps on the same day, so that no legion could help another, and German horsemen had already crossed the Rhine. As a friend, he advised Sabinus to leave at once and promised him a safe road to the nearest camp, only a few days' march away.

Sabinus called all his officers together, and a bitter quarrel began over whether to trust Ambiorix. Cotta and many of the centurions argued that nothing should be done without Caesar's orders, since the camp could hold out against any number of Gauls. Sabinus replied that waiting for help would mean waiting for disaster, and the argument went on far into the night, until at last Cotta gave way.

At dawn the Roman column set out, long and heavy with baggage, and after about two miles it descended into a deep valley, where Ambiorix's men were waiting on the hills on both sides. The Gauls would not come down to fight, but attacked the head and the tail of the column with missiles, and the Romans, hampered by their baggage, could not form a line. Sabinus, who had foreseen nothing, ran about the ranks giving confused orders, while Cotta, who had feared a trap, tried to do the work of a general and a soldier together.

Sabinus, seeing Ambiorix in the distance, sent an interpreter to beg for mercy for himself and his men, and Ambiorix replied that Sabinus might come to him and talk. When Sabinus walked out with his officers, the Gauls surrounded and killed them, and Cotta, wounded by a sling stone, fell soon afterwards, fighting to the last. The standard-bearer Lucius Petrosidius, hard pressed, hurled the eagle into the camp and died fighting in front of it, and the survivors retreated behind the walls.

Despair overcame the survivors in the camp, and during the night they killed one another, so that only a handful escaped through the forests to reach Labienus and tell him what had happened. Ambiorix, delighted with his victory, rode through the night with his cavalry to the Atuatuci, and the next day to the Nervii, urging them to take their revenge and win their freedom. He told them that two Roman officers were dead and that Quintus Cicero's legion could be crushed without trouble.

The Nervii, with the peoples who depended on them, hurried to the winter camp of Quintus Cicero, a brother of the famous orator, and attacked at once, though the soldiers hurried back in time to hold the walls. When this failed, they asked for a meeting, and the Nervian chiefs repeated the arguments of Ambiorix, hoping to lure the Romans out. Cicero, though ill, replied that the Roman people never accepted terms from an enemy under arms, but promised to help the Gauls send envoys to Caesar if they laid down their weapons.

Cicero's men, who had no time to waste, worked through the night with all the timber that they had collected for the camp's defence, and by morning they had built one hundred and twenty towers. They strengthened the rampart, added screens to the battlements and prepared everything that might be needed for a siege. Next day the Nervii attacked in even greater numbers, filling the ditch with brushwood and trying to pull down the rampart, but again the Romans threw them back with heavy losses.

The Gauls had learned a great deal from Roman prisoners, and, though clumsy, they built ramps, siege towers and shelters of their own. As the siege wore on, they began to hurl red-hot clay balls and burning javelins onto the straw roofs of the Roman huts, and a strong wind carried the flames from hut to hut. Although the camp was soon alight, not one Roman left his post, and the soldiers, with blazing huts behind them and a swarm of enemies before them, fought on without a word of complaint.

Two centurions of that legion, Titus Pullo and Lucius Vorenus, had long been rivals for promotion, and each was determined to prove himself the braver. Pullo, in front of the rampart, cried out to Vorenus to ask why he hesitated, and then he charged into the Gauls, only to be wounded and surrounded. Vorenus ran out to save him, and between them they fought their way back inside the walls, so that neither could say which of the two had shown more courage.

Cicero was desperate to send word to Caesar, but every messenger who left the camp was caught and killed in the sight of the garrison. At last a Nervian noble named Vertico, who had fled to the Romans and stayed loyal, persuaded his slave, with a promise of freedom and a large reward, to carry a letter through the enemy lines. The slave, a Gaul himself, passed among the besiegers without raising suspicion, and he brought Cicero's message safely to Caesar.

Caesar received Cicero's letter at about five in the evening, and he at once sent messengers to Crassus and Fabius and to Labienus, ordering them to bring their legions to his aid. At dawn the next day he set out with only two legions, about seven thousand men in all, and after a march of about twenty miles he saw the enemy across a valley and a stream. The Nervii, who had been besieging Cicero with about sixty thousand men, had given up the siege to attack the small Roman force.

Caesar, who had too few men to fight openly, made his camp as small as he could, so that the Gauls would despise him, and he ordered the rampart raised and the gates narrowed. At the same time he sent a Gaulish horseman with a letter, written in Greek so that the enemy could not read it, tied to a javelin that the man hurled into Cicero's camp. The javelin stuck in a tower and was not noticed for two days, but on the third a soldier saw it, and Cicero read the letter aloud to his weary men.

The Gauls, confident that Caesar was afraid, crossed the stream and attacked the little camp, and at a signal the Romans burst out of every gate at once and put them to flight with hardly any loss. The same day Caesar reached Cicero's camp, and he was astonished by what he saw: of the soldiers inside, hardly one in ten was unwounded. He praised Cicero and the legion for their courage, and within hours the news of the rescue was spreading across Gaul.

Indutiomarus, the leader of the Treveri, raised an army and rode up every day to the camp of Labienus, hurling insults at the Romans inside and daring them to come out. Labienus, who had too few men to risk a battle, pretended to be afraid, and he secretly brought cavalry into the camp at night. When the Gauls came up as usual, the Roman horsemen charged out of two gates at once with orders to strike only at Indutiomarus, and they killed him at a river, and his army scattered.

Gaul was restless, and the loss of fifteen cohorts had not gone unnoticed, so Caesar raised two new legions in northern Italy and asked his political partner Pompey to lend him a third. Pompey agreed, and Caesar thus replaced his losses within a few weeks, showing the Gauls what Roman strength could do. Before the winter was over, he had attacked the Nervii and other tribes that had been planning revolt, burning their farms and driving off their cattle.

To show that the Rhine was no barrier to Roman arms, Caesar built a second bridge a little above the first, and the work, which his soldiers now knew well, was finished in a short time. The Ubii, who had given hostages, told him that the Suebi had sent their families into a huge forest called Bacenis, which formed a natural wall between them and the Cherusci. After waiting for some days, Caesar decided that it was not worth the risk of pursuing them so far, and he went back to Gaul, leaving a strong guard at the German end of the bridge.

Here Caesar interrupts his narrative to describe the Gauls, whose tribes, he says, were everywhere divided into rival parties. Only two classes of men counted for anything: the Druids, who were priests, teachers and judges, and the knights, who went to war when they were needed. The common people, crushed by debt and taxes and by the power of the nobles, were almost slaves, and they had no say in public affairs.

The Druids, according to Caesar, judged nearly all disputes, took charge of the sacrifices and taught the sons of the nobles, some of whom stayed with them for as many as twenty years. They believed that the soul does not perish but passes at death into another body, a doctrine that Caesar thought made men braver in war. They would not put their teachings into writing, though the Gauls used Greek letters for ordinary accounts, partly to keep their knowledge secret and partly, he suggests, to keep their students' memories strong.

Caesar says that the Gauls honoured many gods, but he describes them, as a Roman would, in Roman terms. The one that they honoured most, he says, was Mercury, whom they thought the inventor of the arts, and after him came Apollo, Mars, Jupiter and Minerva, who had the same duties as in Rome. Their funerals, he adds, were magnificent, and a man's dearest possessions were burned with him.

The Germans, Caesar tells us, differed from the Gauls in almost every way that he could think of, and he lists the differences with relish. They had no Druids and few sacrifices, and they lived by hunting and war, training their boys from childhood in hardship and cold. No man owned fixed land, for the magistrates shared it out afresh each year, so that no one would grow rich or soft, and a tribe's greatest glory was to have a wide wasteland around its borders.

Caesar describes the great Hercynian Forest, which stretched far to the east from the borders of the Helvetii and was so broad that a man travelling light needed nine days to cross it. Within it lived strange animals, among them a deer with a single horn rising from the middle of its forehead, which was probably a reindeer described at second hand. There was also the elk, which Caesar wrongly believed had no joints in its legs, and the huge aurochs, almost as large as elephants, which the Germans trapped in pits and hunted for glory.

Caesar was determined to punish the Eburones, who had destroyed Sabinus and Cotta, and he invited the neighbouring tribes to plunder their land so that Roman soldiers need not take the risk. Ambiorix himself was hunted through the forests and marshes of the Ardennes, but he escaped over and over again, sometimes by a lucky chance. At other times a few faithful followers died so that he could ride away, and Caesar admits that fortune played a great part, though Ambiorix was never taken.

Caesar had left Quintus Cicero at Atuatuca with a legion and promised to be back in seven days, but the days passed and he did not return. Meanwhile the Sugambri, drawn across the Rhine by the hope of plunder, rode up to the camp and found it almost unguarded, since Cicero had sent five cohorts out to forage. The sick soldiers, led by a centurion named Baculus who rose from his bed to fight, held the gate until the foragers got back, and Caesar later admitted that Fortune had played a great part.

In the early months of 52 BC, riots broke out in Rome after the murder of the politician Clodius, and the Senate ordered every man of military age in Italy to take an oath and join the army. The Gauls, hearing of the disorder, concluded that Caesar would be kept in Italy and could not rejoin his legions. At secret meetings in the forests, the chiefs complained that the freedom of their fathers had been lost, and the Carnutes declared that they would be the first to rise.

On the day they had fixed, two Carnutian leaders went into the town of Cenabum and murdered the Roman traders there, among them Gaius Fufius Cita, who had charge of Caesar's grain supply. The news was passed on by shouting from field to field and village to village, and it reached the country of the Arverni that same evening, more than a hundred miles away. There Vercingetorix, a young man of great influence, heard it and made up his mind to act.

Vercingetorix was the son of Celtillus, who had once held the first place in all Gaul and had been put to death by his own people for aiming at kingship. The young man gathered the poor and the desperate from the countryside, and when his uncle and other nobles refused to join him and drove him out of the town of Gergovia, he went on recruiting. His followers saluted him as king, and he sent envoys to the other states to ask for their support.

From every state that joined him, Vercingetorix demanded a fixed number of soldiers and weapons, and he gave particular attention to cavalry. He ruled with great harshness, punishing the disobedient severely so that the rest would be afraid to question his orders. By these methods he soon gathered the Senones, Parisii, Pictones, Cadurci, Turoni, Aulerci, Lemovices and many others, and they gave him the supreme command.

The news reached Caesar in northern Italy, and he faced a hard choice, since his legions were far away in the north and Gaul was rising between him and them. He therefore hurried to Narbo, in the Province, where Lucterius, one of Vercingetorix's allies, was already threatening the border, and he placed garrisons wherever they were needed. Having steadied the Province, he began to plan how to reach his army before the Gauls could cut it off.

In the depths of winter the Cevennes mountains, which divided the Province from the country of the Arverni, were covered with snow six feet deep, and the Arverni thought that no army could cross them. Caesar urged his soldiers to clear a path by hard labour, and in this way they reached the borders of the Arverni, who were taken completely by surprise. Vercingetorix, afraid for his own land, hurried back, and Caesar, who had wanted just that, rode on to join his legions.

At a council of the Gaulish leaders, Vercingetorix argued that the Romans could not be beaten in the open field, but that they could be starved. Every farm and village within reach of the Roman foragers, he said, must be burned, and every town not strong enough to resist must be burned with them. The loss would hurt, he admitted, but it was far lighter than losing freedom, and the Gauls must choose between burning their property and watching their wives and children carried off as slaves.

The Bituriges set fire to more than twenty of their own towns in a single day, and the other peoples did the same, so that columns of smoke rose on every side. Only Avaricum, which the Bituriges called the finest city in Gaul and the pride of their state, was spared, for they begged on their knees that it should not be burned. Vercingetorix at first refused, but he gave way to their pleading and put a strong garrison inside.

Having rejoined his army, Caesar quickly took the town of Vellaunodunum and marched on to Cenabum, which he reached in two days. The Carnutes were preparing to defend it, but the Romans stormed the gates by night, plundered the town and burned it to avenge the murder of their countrymen. Caesar then crossed the Loire into the land of the Bituriges and marched toward Avaricum.

Caesar camped before Avaricum, but the Gauls had burned everything that might feed his army, and the Boii, who were poor and weak, could send him little. For days the soldiers had no bread at all and lived on the meat of cattle driven in from distant villages, yet no one was heard to say a word unworthy of the Roman people. When Caesar offered to abandon the siege if the labour was too hard, they begged him not to, saying that after so many years under his command they would never leave a task unfinished.

Avaricum was almost surrounded by a river and a marsh, and only a single narrow approach led up to the town. Its wall, in the Gaulish manner, was built of long timbers laid at right angles to one another, with the gaps filled with earth and the face covered with great stones. Fire could hardly harm such a wall, because of the stone, and rams could hardly shake it, because of the timber that bound it together.

While Vercingetorix kept his army in the countryside, near enough to attack the Roman foragers, Caesar's soldiers built their great siege ramp against the wall, working in shifts by day and by night. After twenty-five days it was about three hundred and thirty feet wide and eighty feet high, with towers rising on it. As the great ramp crept toward the wall, the Gauls hurried to find ways to destroy it.

The Bituriges, who had iron mines of their own and knew everything about tunnelling, dug underground passages beneath the ramp and set it on fire from below. They also used iron hooks to pull away the timbers of the Roman shelters, and from towers raised on their wall they hurled burning pitch and tallow. The fighting went on all day and night, and Caesar's men, who had to watch for fire as well as the enemy, were nearly worn out.

On the wall a Gaul stood in front of the gate passing balls of burning tallow and pitch from hand to hand, until a bolt from a Roman catapult struck him down. The man beside him stepped over the body and took his place, and when that man was struck, a third did the same, and so on all through the night. Neither side gave way, and Caesar, who admired courage even in an enemy, thought the scene worth recording.

On the day when the ramp reached the wall, a heavy rain began to fall, and Caesar noticed that the Gaulish guards on the wall had grown careless, thinking that the Romans could not attack in such weather. He ordered his men to go about their work slowly, as if they had no plan, and he quietly told the officers to prepare for an assault. He promised rewards to the first men who climbed the wall, and the soldiers, who had been hungry for weeks, were eager to repay the Gauls.

At the signal the Romans swept up the ramp and over the top of the wall, and the Gauls, who were caught entirely by surprise, were driven from it at once. They gathered in the market-place and in the open ground in a close mass, intending to fight to the last, but when no Roman came down to meet them, they began to fear that they would be surrounded. Then they threw away their arms and rushed for the gates, where they stumbled over one another in the narrow way.

Remembering the murders at Cenabum and the hardships of the siege, the Roman soldiers took no thought for plunder, and they spared neither the old nor women nor children. Of the forty thousand people in the town, according to Caesar, only about eight hundred reached Vercingetorix, who received them quietly and sent them to the camp in small groups so that no one would panic. The Romans found the town full of grain and supplies, and the army was fed again at last.

Vercingetorix, far from being discouraged by the loss, called an assembly and reminded the Gauls that he had never wished to defend Avaricum, which, as he had said, should have been burned like the rest.
