He told them that the Romans had won by an engineering skill that the Gauls had not known, and that victory was certain if all Gaul stood together. Instead of losing the trust of his followers, he gained it, and his army grew with fresh troops from many states.

Two men of the Aedui both claimed to be chief magistrate, and since the quarrel threatened to split that important tribe, Caesar went in person to settle it and to ask for cavalry and grain. He decided in favour of Convictolitavis, and then he divided his army in two, sending Labienus with four legions to deal with the Senones and the Parisii. He himself marched with the other six legions toward Gergovia, the stronghold of the Arverni.

Vercingetorix broke down every bridge over the river Allier and marched along the opposite bank, keeping always in sight of the Romans and making a crossing impossible. Caesar camped in a wood beside the ruins of a bridge and kept back two legions out of sight, while the rest marched on as usual, so that the Gauls, seeing the column, followed it. As soon as they were out of sight, the hidden men rebuilt the bridge on the old piles, and the whole army crossed.

Gergovia stood on the top of a high mountain, and every approach to it was steep, so that Caesar saw at once that it could not be taken by storm. Vercingetorix had set the camp of each tribe on the slope below the walls, and every day he called the Gaulish leaders to a council to decide what to do. Caesar noticed that a hill close to the town was lightly guarded, and in a night attack he captured it and built there a second camp, linked to the main one by a double ditch.

Ten thousand Aeduan infantry set out toward Caesar's camp, led by a young noble called Litaviccus, who had been secretly won over by the Gaulish leaders. At about thirty miles from Gergovia, he halted the column, wept before his men and told them that Caesar had put to death their leading men, Eporedorix and Viridomarus, and all the Aeduan horsemen with them. The soldiers, believing him, robbed the Roman traders who were with them, and sent messengers all through the Aeduan country to stir up revolt.

Eporedorix and Viridomarus, who were with Caesar in the camp, told him what Litaviccus had done, and Caesar, understanding the danger, left two legions behind and marched at once with the other four. After a march of about twenty-five miles, he saw the Aeduan column ahead and sent his cavalry to hold it up, ordering that no man be harmed. Eporedorix and Viridomarus then rode out and showed themselves to their countrymen, and the Aedui, realising that they had been tricked, threw down their arms and surrendered.

Caesar hurried back to Gergovia and found that the Romans in the camp had been fighting all day and were nearly exhausted, while the Gauls, thinking themselves safe in the camps on the slope, grew careless. Then he noticed that the ridge beside the town, crowded the day before, was now almost empty, because the Gauls had moved to the other side to meet a feared attack there. He sent muleteers, wearing helmets, to ride round the hills like cavalry to draw the Gauls' eyes, while the legions crept to the foot of the slope.

At the signal the legions raced up the slope and took three Gaulish camps with such speed that Teutomatus, king of the Nitiobriges, who had been resting at midday, escaped half dressed on a wounded horse. Caesar, content with this success, ordered the retreat to be sounded, and the tenth legion halted, but the soldiers on the left did not hear it over the noise. Carried away by hope of victory, they ran on up the slope and reached the very walls of the town.

From the walls the Gaulish women threw down their clothes and silver and, with arms outstretched, begged the Romans to spare them and not to treat them as the women of Avaricum had been treated. A few soldiers, with the help of their comrades, climbed the wall, and for a short time it seemed as if the town would fall. Then the Gauls who had been guarding the other side of the mountain came pouring back, and the mood changed.

Marcus Petronius, a centurion of the eighth legion, was trying to break down a gate when the Gauls swarmed around him. Seeing that he was wounded and could not save himself, he shouted to his men that, since he could not escape with them, he would at least save the lives of those whom his rashness had brought into danger. He charged at the enemy, killed two of them, and held the rest back long enough for his soldiers to get away, and then he fell.

Lucius Fabius, who had been among the first to climb the wall at Avaricum, was lifted onto the wall by three of his men, and then he pulled others up after him. The Gauls drove them down, and as the Roman line gave way, the tenth legion, stationed by Caesar at the foot of the slope, held the ground and covered the retreat. By the end of the day the Romans had lost forty-six centurions and about seven hundred soldiers.

Next day Caesar called the soldiers together and rebuked them sharply for having ignored the signal to retreat and for acting as if they understood the battle better than their general. He told them that he admired their courage, which no walls or slopes could check, but that he valued obedience and self-control no less than bravery. The soldiers, ashamed, promised to do better, and Caesar then led them out to offer battle on level ground, though the Gauls refused to come down.

News of the defeat at Gergovia encouraged the Aedui, who had been Rome's oldest friends in Gaul, to join Vercingetorix at last. At Noviodunum they killed the Roman traders and seized the hostages, the money and the baggage that Caesar had left there, and then they burned the town so that the Romans could not use it. Caesar, finding the Loire in flood, searched for a ford, crossed with great difficulty and hurried north to join Labienus.

Labienus left Agedincum with four legions and marched down the Seine toward Lutetia, a town of the Parisii on an island in the river, where Vercingetorix's allies were gathering. Their commander was Camulogenus, an old Aulercan chief chosen for his great experience of war, who had camped beyond a vast marsh that no army could easily cross. Labienus tried for some time to build a causeway through the mud, but the work was too difficult, and he gave it up.

Labienus marched in the middle of the night upstream to Metiosedum, another island town in the Seine, taking his four legions with him. There he seized about fifty boats and quickly filled them with soldiers, and the people of the town, who had not expected to see the Romans so soon, surrendered without a fight. He repaired the bridge that the Gauls had broken and led his army across the river.

When Camulogenus heard what had happened, he burned Lutetia and broke down its bridges, and he moved his camp to the river bank directly opposite Labienus. Meanwhile Labienus was told that Caesar had been beaten at Gergovia and that the Aedui had rebelled, and rumours said that the whole of Gaul was in arms. He saw that he could not stay where he was and could not retreat without risking the loss of his army, so he decided to attack.

Labienus ordered five cohorts and all the baggage animals to march noisily upstream, with the boats following them and splashing their oars, so that the Gauls would think that the whole Roman army was moving away. Meanwhile three legions went quietly downstream and crossed the river in the boats at a place where only a few Gauls kept watch. The noise of the false march drew many of the Gauls upstream, and the Romans crossed unseen and landed on the far bank.

On the farther bank the Gauls, who had expected to find no enemy, met the Romans in battle order, and in the fierce fighting that followed, the seventh legion on the right broke the enemy's line and drove them back. Camulogenus himself stood with his men to the last, and he fell fighting, while nearly all the others who stayed with him were killed. Labienus, having won, marched his army back to Agedincum, where he picked up his baggage and rejoined Caesar.

At a great council at Bibracte, the leaders of the Gaulish states confirmed Vercingetorix as commander of the whole war, though the Aedui grumbled that they had a better claim to lead. Vercingetorix demanded fifteen thousand horsemen and hostages from all the peoples, and he explained that the Romans could be beaten without a battle if their grain was cut off and their foragers killed. He also sent the Aedui to ravage the Allobroges, who lived along the border of the Province, to keep the Romans busy.

Caesar had lost the support of his Gallic cavalry, which was a serious blow, so he sent across the Rhine for German horsemen and for light infantry trained to fight among them. The horses that the Germans brought were small and poor, and Caesar took the horses of his officers, and of the Roman knights and veterans, and gave them to the newcomers. With his army complete again, he marched through the land of the Lingones toward the country of the Sequani, so as to be nearer the Province.

Vercingetorix had made his horsemen swear that any man who had not ridden twice through the enemy's line would never again see his home, wife or children. He then drew up his cavalry in three bodies and attacked the Roman column, but Caesar divided his own cavalry into three to meet them, and the fighting broke out on every side. On the right the German horsemen took a ridge and drove the Gauls off it, and the rest of the Gauls, seeing this, fled.

Vercingetorix gave up the battle and led his army toward Alesia, the stronghold of the Mandubii, and the baggage was ordered to come up close behind. Caesar pursued him, killed about three thousand of the Gaulish rearguard, and the next day camped near the town. He then studied the place with great care, and what he saw convinced him that an ordinary assault would fail.

Alesia stood on the top of a lofty hill, so high that it seemed impossible to take except by a long blockade. At the foot of the hill, two rivers flowed along two of its sides, and in front of the town lay a plain about three miles long. On every other side hills of the same height as the town's hill rose close to it, and beneath the wall, on the side facing the rising sun, the Gauls had dug a trench and a six-foot wall.

Before the Romans could close the circle, Vercingetorix called his cavalry together and told them to ride away by night, each to his own people, and to bring every man who could carry a weapon. He reminded them that he had grain for only thirty days, though by strict rationing it might last a little longer, and that he was relying on them for his life and for the freedom of Gaul. The horsemen slipped out in the dark, and the Mandubii and the rest of the army settled down to wait inside the walls.

Caesar saw that Alesia could not be taken by storm, so he decided to starve it out. First there was a fierce cavalry fight on the plain, which went on until sunset, when the German horsemen charged and drove the Gauls back to their walls. Then, with about eighty thousand picked men inside the town, Caesar began to build a ring of siege works around the hill.

The inner line of the Roman works ran for eleven miles around the hill, and along it Caesar built twenty-three forts, where guards stood watch by day against sudden sorties and where sentries were doubled at night. Facing the town was a ditch twenty feet wide with sheer sides, and behind it, on the flat ground, two more ditches, each fifteen feet wide, the inner one filled with water from the river. Behind these rose a rampart twelve feet high, crowned with a palisade and battlements, and with towers every eighty feet.

In front of the ditches, in five rows, the soldiers planted tree trunks with the bark stripped off and the branches sharpened to points, which they called tombstones. Farther out, in a pattern like a chessboard, they dug pits three feet deep, each holding a sharpened stake hardened in fire and hidden under brushwood, and the soldiers called these lilies. In front of them, they buried blocks of wood a foot long, fitted with iron hooks, which they named goads, so that anyone who rushed the Roman line would have to cross a field of traps.

Because he knew that a great army of Gauls might come to the rescue, Caesar built a second line of works of the same kind, facing outward and running for fourteen miles. This outer line was meant to protect the Romans from an attack from behind, so that even a vast army could not surround them. He also gathered grain and fodder for thirty days, so that his men would not have to go out foraging and risk being cut off.

In the Aeduan country, the Gaulish leaders held a council and decided against calling out every man who could carry a weapon, since such a crowd would be impossible to command or to feed. Instead each people was told to send a fixed number of soldiers, and the Aedui and their dependants, the Arverni and many others promised thousands apiece. Altogether, says Caesar, they gathered two hundred and fifty thousand foot soldiers and eight thousand horsemen, though here, as so often, his numbers are probably too big.

Inside Alesia, the day on which help should have come went by without any sign of it, the grain had almost run out, and the people, who knew nothing of what was happening among the Aedui, began to despair. Vercingetorix called a council to discuss what ought to be done, and some of the speakers urged surrender, while others wanted a sortie while strength remained. One speech in that council, however, has been remembered ever since for its savagery, because of the terrible idea that it proposed.

Critognatus, an Arvernian of high birth and great influence, rose to speak against surrender, and Caesar reports his words in full. He reminded the council that their ancestors, besieged by the Cimbri and Teutones and driven by hunger, had kept themselves alive by eating those too weak to fight. He declared that he would rather follow that terrible example than yield, since the Romans wanted nothing but Gaul's land and its freedom, and would never stop until the Gauls were slaves.

The council did not follow Critognatus, but it agreed on a measure that was almost as hard: those who could not fight were to leave the town. The Mandubii, in whose town the whole army had taken refuge, were driven out with their wives and children, so that the food that remained would last a little longer for the soldiers. They went out through the gates and down toward the Roman lines, leaving their homes and their goods behind.

When they reached the Roman lines, the Mandubii begged with tears to be taken in as slaves, if only they could be given food. Caesar, knowing that the same food would otherwise feed the defenders, posted guards along the ramparts with orders to receive no one. They stood between the two armies with nowhere to go, and Caesar does not say what became of them.

At last the Gaulish relief army arrived, led by Commius the Atrebatian, once Caesar's trusted friend, together with the Aedui Viridomarus and Eporedorix and Vercassivellaunus, a cousin of Vercingetorix. It camped on a hill less than a mile from the outer Roman line, and the people of Alesia, seeing their friends on the hills, ran together in great excitement and congratulated one another. Vercingetorix led out his men, who carried hurdles to throw into the ditches, and the Romans, now facing enemies on both sides, stood to arms on both of their lines.

On the first day the Gauls filled the whole plain with cavalry and with archers and light infantry placed among them to support their horsemen, while the people of Alesia crowded the walls to watch. The Roman cavalry, hard pressed, held out until nearly sunset, when the German horsemen charged in a solid body, scattered the archers and drove the Gaulish horse in flight. Disheartened, the defenders of Alesia went back into the town, and the relief army retired to its camp without an attack on the Roman works.

After a day spent making hurdles, ladders and iron hooks, the Gauls crept in the dark toward the outer Roman line and at midnight gave a great shout, which told the besieged in Alesia that the attack had begun. They pelted the Roman rampart with slings and arrows, and tried to fill the ditches, but the Romans under Mark Antony and Gaius Trebonius, who commanded the endangered sections, drove them back with stones, stakes and sling bullets. Many Gauls were wounded by the traps before they ever reached the wall, and they retired before dawn, for fear of being caught in the open.

The Gaulish chiefs sent scouts to look for the weakest place in the Roman lines, and the scouts came back with news of a camp on the northern side. It stood on the slope of a hill that the Romans had been unable to enclose, and the Gauls chose sixty thousand of their best men, under Vercassivellaunus, a cousin of Vercingetorix, to attack it. By night they marched to the hill and hid behind it, waiting for noon.

At about noon, Vercassivellaunus's men came down from behind the hill toward the Roman camp, while the Gaulish cavalry rode out onto the plain and the rest of the relief army moved up to the outer works. The people inside Alesia, seeing the signal, rushed out of the town with their hurdles, ladders and hooks, and Vercingetorix led them against the inner line. All the Romans were forced to defend at once, on a circuit of many miles, with enemies pressing in from both sides and shouting at their backs.

The Romans fought bravely, but they were hard pressed, for the Gauls on both sides hurled so many missiles that the defenders on the towers could scarcely raise their heads. Caesar chose a high place from which he could watch the whole battle, and he sent reserves wherever the danger was greatest. Both sides knew that this was the decisive hour: if the Gauls broke through, the Romans would be lost, and if the Romans held, the Gauls would starve.

On the northern hill, where the Roman camp could not be fully enclosed, the Gauls covered the ditches with earth and hurdles, and they pressed their attack with all their strength. The Romans, tired from the fight and short of missiles, began to give ground, and Caesar sent first Decimus Brutus with a few cohorts and then Gaius Fabius with more. When the fighting grew fiercer still, he decided that he must go there himself, with fresh troops.

Caesar was known to friend and enemy alike by the cloak that he wore in battle, and when he appeared on the slope with fresh troops, a great shout went up from the Roman ranks. The soldiers on the other lines took up the cry, and it echoed from rampart to rampart until both armies understood that the commander was in the fight. At once the soldiers threw aside their javelins and drew their swords, for the cry meant that the decisive struggle had begun.

Labienus, who had managed to collect eleven cohorts from the nearest forts, sent word to Caesar that he could hold no longer and meant to break out and attack. Caesar hurried to join him, and sent some of his cavalry around the outside of the works to take the Gauls in the rear, while he and Labienus led the cohorts forward. The Gauls, surprised to be attacked from behind just as they were pressing the Romans in front, were thrown into confusion and ran.

As the relief army broke, the Roman cavalry rode after it, killed Sedulius, a leader of the Lemovices, and took Vercassivellaunus alive, together with seventy-four military standards. Vercingetorix, who had watched his last hope fail from the walls, led his men back into Alesia, and the fugitives scattered to their homes, so that by dawn the great army of Gaul was gone. Caesar says that if his soldiers had not been so tired after the long day, he could have wiped out the whole force.

Vercingetorix called the people of Alesia together and told them that he had undertaken the war not for his own sake but for the freedom of Gaul, and that they might kill him or give him up as they chose. They sent envoys to Caesar, who ordered them to hand over their weapons and their leaders and sat down in front of his camp, where Vercingetorix was handed over and the weapons were thrown down. Later writers such as Plutarch say that Vercingetorix rode out in his finest armour, circled Caesar's seat and laid down his weapons without a word.

Caesar set aside the prisoners of the Aedui and the Arverni, about twenty thousand men, in the hope of winning back the loyalty of these two powerful peoples. All the other prisoners he gave to his soldiers, one to each man, to be sold as slaves, which was the custom of the time. When his report reached Rome, the Senate decreed twenty days of public thanksgiving, for a war that Rome now believed to be won.

In 51 BC the Bellovaci and a few neighbouring peoples rose once more, and the last of the Gaulish leaders tried to hold out. Caesar, instead of risking a great battle, wore the Bellovaci down by skilful marching and ambushes until their leader Correus was killed and they asked for terms. These events are told in an eighth and final book by Hirtius, an officer who served under Caesar and who wrote it after Caesar's death, to link the Gallic war with the civil war that followed.

The last stronghold to resist was Uxellodunum, a town on a steep hill with a fine spring at its foot, and Caesar, who could not storm it, decided to take away its water. His engineers raised a tower and a ramp to command the spring, and they also dug a secret tunnel to the veins of water that fed it, so that the spring suddenly ran dry. Caesar, who was known for mildness, ordered a cruel punishment for the men who had carried weapons, as a warning, and Hirtius took care to defend it in his book.

Hirtius says that Caesar's last year in Gaul was spent in keeping the peace by gentle means. He treated the states with respect, loaded their leaders with gifts and laid no new burdens on them, so that a land worn out by war would have no reason to rise again. Other ancient writers add that Caesar took great wealth from Gaul, and that the war made him rich and powerful as well as famous.

Vercingetorix was kept a prisoner for about six years, and he was never allowed to see Gaul again. In 46 BC, after the civil war that had made Caesar master of Rome, he was led in chains through the city in the triumph that celebrated Caesar's victories in Gaul. According to the historian Cassius Dio, who wrote long afterwards, he was put to death when the procession was over.

In 49 BC, when his enemies in the Senate demanded that he give up his army, Caesar led it across the Rubicon into Italy, and the civil war began. Veterans of the Gallic wars and many Gaulish horsemen fought beside him, and by 46 BC he was master of the Roman world. In 44 BC he was murdered by a group of senators on the Ides of March, and the man who had conquered Gaul fell in the city that he ruled.

Caesar wrote the Gallic War himself, and he refers to himself throughout as Caesar, which makes the narrative sound calm, objective and fair. The great orator Cicero admired it, saying that it was plain, straightforward and graceful, stripped of every ornament. But it was written to be read in Rome by voters and senators, and it shows only the side of the man who won.

Many of Caesar's numbers, from the three hundred and sixty-eight thousand Helvetii to the quarter of a million Gauls at Alesia, are probably too large, and modern historians treat them with caution. Other evidence supports him in part, for in the 1860s, on the orders of Napoleon the Third, diggers found Roman ditches, pits and weapons at Alise-Sainte-Reine that match his description of Alesia. More digging in the 1990s confirmed the site, and some ancient writers claimed that about a million people died in the Gallic wars, though nobody can know the true figure.

After eight years of war, Gaul had become a Roman land, and the roads that Caesar's soldiers had built began to carry traders, officials and teachers where they had once carried armies. Within a few generations the Gauls had adopted Latin and Roman customs, and in the year 48 the emperor Claudius, who had been born in the Gaulish city of Lugdunum, welcomed Gaulish nobles into the Roman Senate. In time the land of Vercingetorix became France, whose language is still a child of Latin, and Caesar's book remains the first account of how that began, though it tells only his side.
